en: The *Miaofa Lianhua Jing Zhizhang Shu*: Exegesis on the Meaning of the Events [of the Lotus Sutra].
△ Preliminary Exposition:
Do Not Despise This Leisurely Occasion.
The Master said, "As for Yu, I have no fault to find with him. The commentary states: "Xiàn (閒) refers to a crack or flaw;
it means to point out his flaws and criticize him. This is found in the *Analects*, Part One.
The phrase "hanging one and missing ten" is seen in the *New Gazetteer of Putuo*, meaning that what was taken up was little while what was omitted was much. The pestle, mortar,
rope, and winnowing basket all speak of the resemblance to the body of an elephant.
The *Nirvāṇa Sūtra*, fascicle thirty-two, states: "For example, there was a king who told a high minister to assemble many blind men and show them an elephant.
At that time, those blind men each touched it with their hands. The king called the blind men together and questioned them one by one."
As for what kind of creature the elephant is: he who touches its tusks says the elephant's shape is like a radish root;
he who touches its ears says the elephant is like a winnowing basket; he who touches its head says the elephant is like a rock; he who touches its trunk says the elephant is like a pestle.
Those who touched its feet said the elephant was like a mortar; those who touched its back said it was like a bed; those who touched its belly said it was like a jar;
and those who touched its tail said it was like a rope. The commentary states: In that sutra, the king is likened to the Tathāgata;
the ministers to the Mahāparinirvāṇa Sūtra; the elephant to the Buddha-nature; and the blind men to all sentient beings shrouded in ignorance. Now...
The meaning of the sūtra can be inferred by analogy.
[The question arises: "Which clarifies the true color of milk—swan-feathers, snow, conch-shells, or rice?
The *Nirvāṇa Sūtra*, fascicle 14, states: "It is like a person born blind who does not know the color of milk and asks another, 'What is the color of milk?'"
"What is the color like? The other replied, "The color is white, like a conch shell. The blind man asked again, "Does this milk-colored thing have a sound like that of a conch shell?
He replied, "No. He asked again, "What is the color of the conch shell like? He replied, "It is like rice flour.
The blind man asked again, "Is the milk-colored thing as soft as rice flour? And what is rice flour like?"
[The questioner] asks what it resembles. He replies, "It is like snow or rain. The blind man asks again, "Is that rice flour as cold as snow?
[The questioner asks], "And what does snow resemble? He replies, "It is like a white crane.

Although this person born blind has heard these four kinds of analogies, he is ultimately unable to recognize the true color of the milk. These non-Buddhists (*tīrthika*) are also just like this; they will never...

One can thereby attain the permanence, bliss, self, and purity. I have now extracted this from the commentary because it serves as an analogy showing that while other schools possess only mere words, they entirely lack the true meaning;
their paths are divergent and obstructed.
Jianwu asked Lianshu: "I heard the words of Jieyu; they were grand yet without substance, departing and never returning.
I was struck with awe by his speech, which was as vast and boundless as the Milky Way. It was so immense and extraordinary that it did not accord with human nature.
(The commentary notes: "Distant as the earth and sky" refers to the great distance between them. See the "Free and Easy Wandering" chapter of the *Zhuangzi*.)
The *Jiankou Jiayu* states: When Confucius visited Zhou, he entered the temple of Houji and beheld a golden man with his three orifices sealed shut. Inscribed upon its back was this:
"If the mechanism of Heaven is not kept secret, how can the four seasons proceed? If the mechanism of Earth is not kept secret, how can the myriad things [flourish]?"
Life begins. If the human mechanism is not sealed, how can any of the hundred affairs be accomplished? The commentary states: "Sealed" means to close or seal up.

Regarding the handle of the axe, there is a method; as the poem says: "To hew the axe-handle, to hew the axe-handle—the model for it is not far off. The commentary states: "The handle" refers to the shaft of an axe; "the model" refers to the standard or rule. This means...
In felling a handle for an axe, one does not err by taking this old axe-handle as the standard to obtain the measure for a new handle.
See the "Fà Kē" (Felling the Handle) chapter of the *Bīngfēng* (The Airs of Bīng).

Regarding the reliance upon one's kin, a poem says: "Without a father, on whom can one rely? Without a mother, on whom can one depend? The commentary states: "To rely" means to take as a support; "to depend" means to count upon.
Regarding the statement that there is "no father and no mother," upon what does one rely? Looking at the chapter "Liao'e" (The Arundel Grass) in the *Xiaoya*, it says:

"The ant’s pace and the measure of a conch shell [are insufficient for] the lotus pond. Master Nanyang Huizhong said: "The mountain for ants and the wind and water [for fish] distinguish between difficulty and ease. The meaning is that practicing through other gates is like this.
An ant climbing a high mountain and reciting the Buddha’s name to attain rebirth in the Pure Land is like a wind-blown sail sailing upon a following current.

The *Biography of Dongfang Shuo* of the Han Dynasty states: "Using a conch shell to measure the ocean. Xunzi says this refers to the shallowness of what one perceives. The *Dictionary* explains that *lí* (蠡) refers to a conch shell.
[The character] is pronounced *lí* (as in *lián-tí*). It refers to a gourd used as a ladle.
Regarding the "King's Way" (*wáng-dào*), it is broad and level;

its principles have been the same for a thousand ages. The *Huánjì* states: "The King penetrates the Three Powers (*sān-cái*), presides over the myriad things, transforms the world through non-action (*wú-wéi*), and bestows grace upon the people through the Way."
"Tantan" means level and vast. Being both level and vast, who throughout the ages has not followed this same standard?
The *Nirvāṇa Sūtra*, fascicle twenty-seven, states: "For example, there is a poor man whose house contains a treasure storehouse; yet because he does not see it..."
Therein is no permanence, no bliss, no self, and no purity. Yet there exists a spiritual friend who employs skillful means to cause one to see them;
because of this vision, that person immediately attains permanence, bliss, self, and purity.

A verse from the Avataṃsaka Sūtra within the *Dhūli-paṭala* (The Chapter on Dust) says: Suppose there were a great scripture, its size equal to the Great Trichiliocosm, contained within a single mote of dust;
and so it is with every mote of dust. A person of wisdom and clear vision perceives it all distinctly; they break open the mote and bring forth the scripture.
It brings vast benefit to sentient beings. The Buddha-wisdom is likewise: it pervades the minds of all sentient beings, yet they are entangled by deluded thoughts;
thus they neither perceive nor know it. Out of great compassion, the Buddhas cause them to eliminate these deluded thoughts, and in this way, [the wisdom] manifests.
It benefits all bodhisattvas; see the fifty-first fascicle.
Who would be willing to lightly grant the "City of Ten Thousand Li"?
Zhao possessed the Bianhe Jade. King Zhao of Qin wished to trade for it with twelve cities of ten thousand li. Zhao dispatched his Chancellor...
As he delivered it, he observed that King Qin possessed only a desire for the jade璧 (bi) and lacked any intention to cede the city.
He then feigned a remark, saying, "The jade has a flaw; please allow me to point it out. The King handed the jade to Xiàng Rú.

Xiàng Rú leaned against a pillar and stood there, his hair bristling in anger as he exclaimed, "I have heard that even among commoners, those who form a bond of friendship cannot bear to deceive one another; how much less so in the case of a great state! The King—
"If you are in haste, my lord, let my head and the jade璧 (bi) both shatter against the pillar. Fearing that the jade璧 might be destroyed, the King allowed him to return to Zhao.
A later poem by Xian says: "The Buan jade is flawless, its brilliance outshining the sun; Though the King of Qin cherished it, he did not yield his stratagem.

Pitifully, it again fell into the hands of Zhang Qiu; A single gust of pure wind carried it back home along the road. This is seen in the *Records of the Grand Historian* (*Shiji*) and the *Chronicles of the Warring States* (*Lieguo Zhi*).

Regarding the statement that all waters flow toward the sea, the *Xia Shu* (Book of Xia), in the chapter "Yu Gong" (The Tribute of Yu), says: "The Yangtze and Han rivers flow toward and pay homage to the sea. The commentary states: "Appearing [before the ruler] in spring is called 'chao' (audience);

appearing in summer is called 'zong' (homage). 'Chaozong' is the name for the audiences held by feudal lords when they visit the Son of Heaven. The Yangtze and Han rivers converge at Jing, and from there they proceed to the sea.
It is still far off; yet the waterways are already settled, free from the calamities of blockages or sudden breaches.
Although it has not yet reached the sea, its momentum is already surging toward it, much like the feudal lords paying court to their sovereign.
The *Yuzi Anluo Mituo Shuchao* states: "Fish are scaly insects; their offspring are numerous, yet those that reach maturity are few. 'Anluo' is the name of a fruit.
In Sanskrit it is called *āmra*, which here is translated as 'difficult to distinguish. Its fruit resembles a peach or a pear, and it is difficult to tell whether it is ripe or unripe."

These flowers are many, yet they produce few fruits. Thus a sutra says: "The eggs of fish, the *āmra* flower, and the Bodhisattva’s initial resolve—these three things are abundant in their causal stage, yet when the fruit is attained, they are few."

The *Yanyi* (Exegesis) on the *Shuchao* (Sub-commentary) to the *Amitābha Sūtra* states: "Śāriputra had already attained the sixth stage (*ṣaṣṭha-bhūmi*) of the Separate Teaching (*pratyekabuddha-yāna*) after having resolved his mind upon Bodhi.
Because Śakra, having transformed himself into a Brahmin, begged him for his eyes, Śāriputra gave them to him. The Brahmin..."

They abandoned the ground and trampled it; because of this, they fell away from the Great Mind (*mahācitta*). For aeons as numerous as motes of dust, they have remained fallen in the stage of the Śrāvaka.
The Chan Master Wuxi of Tang, Wuzhuo, was traveling to Mount Wutai when he paused briefly before Huayan Temple. There he encountered an old man.
A plowman approached him and asked, "Where do you wish to go? Asanga replied, "I wish to enter the Vajra Cave, but I cannot find its door.
The man said, "Stay at my house for a short while and drink some tea. Asanga followed him for more than fifty paces.

He arrived at the man’s house. The man invited him to sit and asked, "Where have you come from recently? Zhe replied, "From the South. The man asked, "How is the Buddha-dharma maintained in the South?
Zhe replied, "The bhikṣus there pay little heed to the Vinaya. The man asked, "How large is the assembly? Zhe replied:
There were sometimes three hundred, sometimes five hundred. Zhe asked, "How is the Dharma maintained here? The old man replied, "Dragons and snakes are mixed;
ordinary people and sages intermingle. Zhe asked, "How many followers are there? The old man replied, "Three times three before, three times three after.
(See the *New Gazetteer of Qingliang*.)

"Like the sound of metal and the resonance of jade," said Mencius, "is what is meant by 'the Grand Synthesis' ascribed to Confucius. This 'Grand Synthesis' consists in sounding the metal bell and concluding with the resonance of jade.
Sounding the metal bell represents the beginning of the systematic order; the resonance of jade represents the completion of that systematic order. (Commentary)
It is said: "The golden bell (*jinzhong*) represents 'proclamation' (*xuan*); the jade chime (*yuqing*) represents 'conclusion' (*shou*').
This means that when music is performed, one first strikes the bell before it begins to proclaim its commencement, and waits until it has ended to ring the chime to conclude it."

In the *Mencius*, Chapter on Wan Zhang (Alcove 1), it is said: "Clouds and dragons, wind and tigers. Regarding the *Book of Changes*, *Qian Hexagram*, line 9-5: "The flying dragon is in the heavens; it is advantageous to see the great man. What does this mean? Confucius replied: "Yin and yang are the Way of Heaven; the four seasons are the Way of Heaven; the hundred grains are the Way of Heaven; the sun and moon are the Way of Heaven; the stars and constellations are the Way of Heaven; the emergence of sages is the Way of Heaven. When the Way of Heaven is established, the Way of Man is established. When the Way of Man is established, the Way of Heaven is established. Therefore, when the Way of Heaven is established, the Way of Man is established; when the Way of Man is established, the Way of Heaven is established. Thus, the sage follows the Way of Heaven to establish the Way of Man. This is what is meant by 'the flying dragon is in the heavens; it is advantageous to see the great man.'"* *Note: The passage provided in the prompt appears to be a composite of several classical texts. The first sentence refers to the *Mencius*, Wan Zhang 1. The second sentence quotes the *Book of Changes*, Qian Hexagram, line 9-5. The subsequent dialogue is a paraphrased or expanded version of the response given by Confucius to Meng Zhixiang regarding the significance of the "flying dragon" and the "great man," as recorded in the *Analects*, Yan Yuan.*
It is said: "Those of the same sound respond to one another; those of the same breath seek one another out. Water flows toward moisture; fire moves toward dryness.

Clouds follow the dragon; wind follows the tiger. When the Sage arises, all things behold him. The commentary on the text states: "Wherever sounds are identical, this one must sing and that one must harmonize, so they respond to each other.
Wherever breaths are identical, this one must bestow and that one must receive, so they seek one another out. It further states: "The dragon is an aquatic creature; the cloud is..."
Water is vapor; thus, when the dragon roars, clouds rise. The tiger is a beast of fierce majesty; thus, when the tiger howls, the wind arises.
When Ziqi passed away, Boya broke his strings.
The *Lüanzi*, "Tangwen" chapter, states: "Yuy Boya was skilled at playing the qin, and Zhong Ziqi was skilled at listening. Boya played..."
Qin was playing his zither with his mind set upon the high mountains. Ziqi said, "How magnificent! It is like Mount Tai.
When his mind was set upon flowing water, Ziqi said, "How beautiful! It is vast and expansive, like the Yangtze and the Yellow River. Whatever Bo Ya contemplated, Ziqi invariably knew.
Later, when Ziqi died, Bo Ya never played the zither again for the rest of his life. Why? Because there was no one who could understand him.
The *Zhongyong* says:
"Therefore, when Heaven produces things, it necessarily accords with their material and treats them with thickness. Thus, that which is planted is nourished; that which is leaning is overturned.
The commentary states: "Material" refers to the substance; "thick" means abundant; "planting" means establishing. When the vital energy (*qi*) arrives, they flourish and grow.
It is for the sake of cultivation. When the vital energy (*qi*) turns back and wanders away, it becomes overturned.

Regarding this, the *Líjì* (Book of Rites), *Qūlǐ* (Etiquette of Curved Rites), states: "Do not plagiarize; do not echo. The commentary notes: "Do not plagiarize or appropriate established doctrines; do not [speak] like an echo."
To merely conform to the words of others is likely to follow their right and wrong, lacking any settled judgment.

Regarding the statement that "the sounds of *fàn* (Sanskrit) differ between the regions of Chu and Xia," the *Yòuxué* (Elementary Learning) says: "Chu has three [divisions]: Dongchu (East Chu), Nanchu (South Chu), and Xichu (West Chu). Since Xiongqú enfeoffed his son Héng as..."

The Prince of E. Originally named E-zhu, it was called Jiangxia during the Han dynasty; when the Wu state made this its capital, it was called Wuchang. This is the present-day province of Hubei and Hunan. "Xia" refers to the Huaxia (the Chinese people);
it is also called Zhongzhou (the Central Region) or Zhongyuan (the Central Plains). Since King Cheng of Zhou established his capital at Luo, [this region has remained central].
Upon the relocation of King Ping to the East, it first became established here. The Qin called it Sanchuan; the Han called it Luoyang; the Tang called it Dongdu;
and the Song called it Xijing—this is present-day Henan Province. What differs [between these eras] refers to the dialects and pronunciations of the Chu and Xia regions.

The variations in tone—light and heavy, or high and low—are different. The Sanskrit sounds of the Western Regions are similar to this; it is because the Central Kingdom (Madhyadeśa) is like the Middle Plain (Zhongxia), while the other four regions are like the three dialects of Chu, that it is said so.
The sacred teachings of this region are called "Classics" (*jing*).
These sacred teachings of this region refer specifically to the teachings of Confucius. They are termed "Classics" such as the *Shi*, *Shu*, *Li*, *Yi*, and *Chunqiu*.

These are called the Five Classics. Since the Sūtra is a sacred teaching from the Western Regions, it is also translated as "Jing" (Classic). This is seen in the *Huayan Xuantan* (Prolegomena to the Avataṃsaka).
Point A conforms [to the original], while Point B deviates.
This refers to the various schools' systems of doctrinal classification, which differ from one another like those of person A and person B;
if one follows this system, it contradicts that, and if one conforms to that, it contradicts this.
The *Seventy-five Dharmas of the Tripiṭaka* states: "In the teachings of the Hīnayāna, seventy-five dharmas are subsumed into five categories, namely:

matter (*rūpa*), mind (*citta*), mental factors (*caitta*), non-associated formations (*viprayukta-saṃskāra*), and unconditioned phenomena (*asaṃskṛta*). The *Abhidharmakośakārikā* says: "Matter-dharmas are eleven; mind-dharmas are one; [mental factors are forty-six];..."

There are sixteen types of mental factors (*caitta-dharma*), fourteen types of dissociated phenomena (*viprayukta-saṃskāra*), and three types of unconditioned phenomena (*asaṃskṛta*), totaling seventy-five.
The first stage (*bhūmi*) consists of eight;
as the fourth chapter of the *Laṅkāvatāra Sūtra* states: "The first stage consists of eight, and the ninth consists of seven; these seven likewise become..."
8. The second becomes the third; the fourth becomes the fifth; the third becomes the sixth. As for "nothingness," what sequence could there be? The commentary states:
"In the Sudden Teaching (Tonjō), stages are not established; therefore, mutual interchange is permitted. The concluding remark, "As for 'nothingness,' what sequence could there be?
means that since everything is simultaneously discarded, what need is there to discuss order?
The *Vimalakīrtinirdeśa-sūtra* states: "Thereupon, Mañjuśrī asked Vimalakīrti: 'We have each spoken according to our own understanding;
now, O Benevolent One, you should speak. What is the entrance into the Dharma-gate of non-duality? At that time, Vimalakīrti remained silent."
There was silence. Mañjuśrī praised him, saying: "Excellent, excellent! To be without even words and letters—this is the true entrance into the Dharma-gate of non-duality."
Carrying Hemp and Discarding Gold:
In the past, there were two men who entered the mountains to pursue their livelihoods, each carrying a load of hemp. By chance, they encountered countless bolts of cloth along the way.
One wise man said, "I shall discard my hemp and take the cloth. The other, a foolish man, said, "I shall carry it back the way we came."

They traveled a short distance and saw nothing but hemp. After going a little further, they encountered silver; the wise man discarded his cloth and carried the silver, while the fool continued as before to carry the hemp.
Going forward again, they encountered gold; the wise man discarded the silver and carried the gold, while the fool continued as before to carry only the hemp.
Those who rely solely on their own views and refuse to follow others are for the most part like this. Thus it is seen.
The *Amitābha-yanyì* (Exegesis on Amitābha).
Regarding the "Metaphor of Eating Vajra" from the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra*, fascicle 52, it says: "For example, if a man eats a small amount of vajra, it will ultimately never be digested."
It must pierce through his body and emerge on the outside. Why is this? Because the diamond [nature] does not coexist with the impurities of the physical body.
It is likewise with even a small root of goodness planted toward the Tathāgata:

it must pierce through the entire body of afflictions consisting of all conditioned formations (*saṃskāra*) and reach the state of ultimate unconditioned wisdom (*asaṃskṛta-jñāna*). Why is this? Because this small...
Roots of goodness do not coexist with the afflictions of conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*).
As Mencius said: "One who is self-destructive cannot be spoken to; one who is self-abandoning cannot be engaged in action."

Furthermore, to say that one does not conform to ritual and righteousness is called "self-sabotage"; to say that one’s own person cannot abide in benevolence or follow righteousness is called "self-abandonment.
This is seen in the "Liyou" (Li Lou) chapter.

The sixth fascicle of the *Sūtra on the Ocean-like Samādhi of Quickly Beholding the Buddha in Subsequent Lives* states: In the city of Śrāvastī, at the home of the elder Sudatta, there was an old woman who did not wish to see the Buddha.
When the Buddha stood before her, she shielded herself with a fan. The Buddha caused the fan to become like a mirror.
There was no obstruction whatsoever; in the four directions, above, and below, all were entirely Buddhas. He covered his face with his hand, and all ten fingers transformed into Buddhas.
The old mother did not believe it, so the Buddha had Rāhula deliver her. Rāhula then transformed himself into a Wheel-Turning Sage King (Cakravartin).
He went to the householder’s home and proclaimed the sublime Dharma. Upon hearing it, the old woman felt great joy;
she then went to the Buddha’s dwelling, left the household life, received full ordination, and attained the realization of the fruits [of the path].

King Prasenajit said to the Buddha, "What sins did this mother commit in her past lives to be born into such a lowly station? And what blessings and merit does she possess that she now encounters the World-Honored One? The Buddha said, "In the past, there was a Buddha named..."
After the parinirvāṇa of the Buddha Ratnacchatradīparāja, during the period of the Semblance Dharma, there was a king named Citraratnapuṣpaprabha.
He had a son named Kṣipradarśana who wished to leave the household life; the king immediately granted him permission. On a mountain there was a bhikṣu.
He became my disciple. He slandered his teacher, claiming he was empty and lacked wisdom, saying, "I pray that in future lives I may never again behold him.
He said, "My *ācārya* possesses wisdom and eloquence; I pray that in every birth he may be my spiritual friend (*kalyāṇamitra*).

Because of his erroneous understanding, after his life ended, he fell into the Avīci Hell. At that time, the *upādhyāya* was none other than my current self; the *ācārya* was none other than the present Rāhula.
Yunshi is [the one who said this]. The bhikṣu Kuàijiàn is none other than the old mother here now.
*Preface to the Wide Dissemination:
A Verse by Cízào*
The Verse says: The Great Master of the Southern Mountain was most profound and mysterious; he distilled the essential pivot and placed it before the sutras.
The Celestial General Vaiśravaṇa personally bestowed his report, and the Buddhas of the ten directions authorized the Master’s words.

Regarding the Yuan Daozhe Mountain where the Elder Xiangmai resided: Yunfeng Temple. As for the rustic elder Xiangmai of Ruyi, he was a native of Taiyuan. Internally, he exhausted the mastery of the Tripiṭaka;
externally, he scrutinized the Nine Schools of thought. He once engaged in debate with the Daoist Qiu Chuji and others concerning the truth or falsehood [of their doctrines]. At that time...
In the eighteenth year of the Yuan dynasty, on the twentieth day of the tenth month, by imperial decree, the scriptures were burned; thus, both Daoist and Buddhist texts were destroyed.

Consequently, the Sun of the Buddha shone once more with renewed brilliance. [Dao’an] previously composed the *Bianwei lu* (Record of Distinguishing the False) in five fascicles, which was included in the canon and circulated widely; this is detailed in the preface to that record.

The *Guānzhōng Jì* (Record of Guanzhong) states that the Han capital was Chang’an. To the east lies the Hangu Pass; to the south, the Rong Pass and Wuguan Pass; to the west, the San Pass; and to the north, the Xiao Pass.
Because it is situated in the midst of these four passes, it is named Guanzhong. This is seen in the *Zhèngzītōng*. "Jì" (Record) refers to a chronicle or historical record.

Master Sengyou, the Vinaya Master, was surnamed Yu. His ancestors were from Xiapi in Pengcheng, though his father had lived in Jianye for generations. He took refuge in the Dharma under Dharma Master Fada of Dinglin Temple;
upon reaching the required age, he received full ordination. He maintained firm and clear principles in his conduct and studied the Vinaya under Dharma Master Faying.

The Master was profoundly disciplined in the Vinaya. During the reign of Emperor Wenxuan of the Qi dynasty, he was invited to lecture on the Vinaya, with a constant audience of seven or eight hundred people.

During the Yongming era, by imperial decree, he was tested and selected among the five assemblies to proclaim and lecture on the *Sarvāstivāda-vinaya* (Shisong lü), further extending the methods for receiving the precepts.

When he grew old and suffered from foot ailments, an imperial edict ordered a palanquin to bring him into the inner palace to confer the precepts upon the ladies of the six quarters. He was also honored by the Princes of Linchuan and Nanping of the Liang dynasty.
He concurrently venerated the precepts and models of conduct. In the seventeenth year of the Tianjian era, he manifested his passing at Jianchu Monastery at the age of seventy-four.

He authored the *Sanzang ji* (Records of the Tripitaka), the *Fayuan ji* (Records of the Dharma Garden), the *Shijie ji* (Records of the World), the *Shijia pu* (Genealogy of Śākyamuni), and the *Hongming ji* (Collection for the Propagation and Clarification of Buddhism); all of these circulate in the world.
A detailed account may be found in the eleventh fascicle of the *Gaoseng zhuan* (Biographies of Eminent Monks).
When one picks up the brush and reads the biographies, even great scholars acknowledge his mastery;
as for the praise offered by the Indian monks, the *Fozu Tongzai* states: "Master Daoxuan was a native of Dantu (alternatively said to be Changcheng).
At the age of fifteen, he followed Master Ying of Riyang to receive his training. At twenty, he followed Vinaya Master Zhishou of Hongfu Monastery."

He was fully ordained. He further studied the Vinaya under his primary teacher and, by nature, was inclined toward *dhyāna*, vowing to cultivate right concentration. Master Yǒn said, "Only when the precepts are pure and concentration is clear does wisdom have a basis.

At the beginning of your studies, you are not yet proficient; how can you distinguish between what is maintained and what is transgressed? Later, he moved to Zhūmálánkǔ on Mount Zhōngnán, where he composed the *Xíngshì Chāo* (Commentary on Monastic Practice).

When the master had completed the construction of the ordination platform (*sīmāmaṇḍala*), a foreign monk suddenly appeared, prostrated before the platform, and praised it, saying: [The rest of the passage continues with the monk's praise.]
Since the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa, during the period when the Semblance Dharma (śāsanapratirūpaka) abides in the world, you alone have brought forth the Vinaya.
"Gū" refers to a bamboo tablet. Lu Shiheng’s *Wenfu* states: "Some grasp the gū and compose with haste. Those who excel at composition today are said to "dip the brush and grasp the gū."

"I transmit but do not create. The Master said: "I transmit but do not create; I trust in and love antiquity. I venture to compare myself to our Old Peng. The commentary states: "To 'transmit' means merely to pass on what is old;
'to create' means to initiate something new. Therefore, creating requires nothing less than a sage, whereas transmitting can be accomplished by the worthy."
"Can be reached" is a term used for those held in high esteem; "I" is a term used for those held dear. Lao Peng was a virtuous Great Officer of the Shang dynasty;
this is likely the modest language of a sage. This is seen in the *Analects*, Part One.

When the barbarians brought disorder to the Central Kingdom, the Emperor said, "Gao Yao! Since the barbarians bring disorder to the Central Kingdom, and there are robbers, thieves, and traitors, you shall serve as the Minister of Justice. For the five types of offenses, there shall be corresponding punishments.

The commentary states: "Hua" (猾) means "to cause disorder"; "Xia" (夏) refers to that which is bright and great. Master Zeng said: "The Central Kingdom is a land of civilization; therefore, it is called 'Hua' (the Flowering)."

"Xia" (Summer). This refers to the summer among the four seasons; it also takes this same meaning. One who abducts people is called a "kǒu" (marauder); one who kills people is called a "zéi" (bandit). One who acts outside [the borders] is called a "jiān" (intruder);

one who acts within [the realm] is called a "yǒu" (rebel). "Shì" (gentleman) means "to govern" (lǐ). "Fú" (to wear/submit) means to submit to one's crime. This is seen in the "Shun Dian" (Canon of Shun) of the Book of Documents.
Zhen is the hexagram of the East.

The *Appended Statements* of the *Book of Changes* (*Zhouyi*) says: "The Supreme Ultimate gives birth to the Two Polarities; the Two Polarities give birth to the Four Images; the Four Images give birth to the Eight Trigrams."
First is Qian, in the northwest. Second is Kan, in the due north. Third is Gen, in the northeast. Fourth is Zhen, in the due east.
Fifth is Xun, in the southeast. Sixth is Li, in the due south. Seventh is Kun, in the southwest. Eighth is Chong, in the due west.
"Zǎi" (carried) is also a term for "year. The *Erya* states: "In the Xia dynasty it was called suì (age); in the Shang, sì (sacrifice); in the Zhou, nián (year); and in the Tang and Yù, zǎi.

This is because "zǎi" takes its meaning from the completion of things and the beginning of anew; "suì" derives from the stars completing their cycle in one year; "sì" from the sacrifices being completed throughout the year; and "nián" [from the grain ripening].
Because grain ripens in one year, these four [seasons] differ in name but are identical in substance.
The East belongs to the Green;
its movement is Wood, its color is green, its constant virtue is benevolence, its flavor is sour, and its organ is the liver. These are the four virtues.

The Origin: At that time, it is spring. It opens its orifice at the eyes. Furthermore, the *Huangdi Sushu Wen* says: "The five viscera correspond to the four seasons; each has its respective reception.
Qibō replied: "Yes. In the east, the color is blue; it enters and communicates with the liver. Its orifice opens at the eyes.
Its taste is sour; its musical note is Jiao."
Shao Ping Planted Melons.
Shao Ping was the Marquis of Dongling during the Qin dynasty. When the Qin was extinguished, he became a commoner and planted melons east of the city of Chang’an;
thus, they are called Dongling melons by the world. Another account calls them Qingmen melons. A later worthy composed a poem saying: "The Han King raised..."

The sword extinguished the solitary Qin; all the lords of the fallen state became his subjects. Only Dongling was able to maintain his integrity, willingly becoming a man who plants melons at the Green Gate.
This is seen in the *History of Han* and recorded in various historical accounts.
"The Tribute of Yu, the Domain of Yongzhou.
"The Tribute of Yu" (*Yugong*) is the title of a chapter in the *Book of Yu* (*Xia shu*). "Yongzhou" is one of the Nine Provinces. The Book states:

"Within the Black Water and west of the River lies Yongzhou. The commentary explains: "The domain of Yongzhou is bounded by the Black Water to the west and reaches the West River to the east; it is therefore called 'West River' (*Xi he*)."

This refers to the capital of Jidu. The Nine Provinces are as follows: Ji Province, Yan Province, Qing Province, Xu Province, Yang Province, Jing Province, Yu Province, Liang Province, and Yong Province. These are they.
During the period of the Five Barbarians’ Turmoil in China:
Liu Yuan of the Former Zhao resided in Pingyang; Shi Le of the Later Zhao resided in Xiangyang; Fu Jian of the Former Qin and Yao Chang of the Later Qin both resided in Chang’an;
and Murong Jun of the Former Yan occupied Ye. This is as seen in the *Jian-shu* (Book of Mirrors), as well as during the Eastern and Western Jin dynasties.

The poem regarding one's native village says: "As for the mulberry and the catalpa trees, one must certainly treat them with reverence. The commentary states: "Catalpa and mulberry are the names of two types of trees.

In ancient times, five-mu plots of land were provided within the residential compounds; these trees were planted beneath the walls to be passed down to descendants, to provide fodder for silkworms and to supply household utensils. Thus, the descendants maintain [them]."
One must certainly pay them reverence. See the "Xiǎobàn" chapter of the *Xiǎoyǎ*. The present term "Zǐlǐ" (Sandalwood Village) refers to the place where one's Great Master was born;
it is the land where one's parents planted the *sān* and *zǐ* trees.

The Fourth Patriarch, Venerable Upagupta, was a native of the kingdom of Takṣaśilā. During his lifetime, he guided and transformed beings, and those who attained the fruits of realization were most numerous.
Whenever he delivered one person, he would place a tally-stick in a stone chamber. That chamber was eighteen cubits in length and ten [cubits] in width.

Two cubits [in height], filling the space between them. Seeing this in the *Record of the Transmission of the Lamp*, [one recalls] the "burnt sprouts and ruined seeds," the "lame tortoises and crippled donkeys.
In the *Vimalakīrti Sūtra*, Kāśyapa reproaches himself, saying: "Why have we forever severed our roots regarding this Mahāyāna?"
"They are like spoiled seeds. The commentary explains: "Spoiled seeds" are seeds that have already been damaged and are incapable of sprouting.

It is likewise with those of the Two Vehicles (*dvayayāna*), who, having extinguished their bodies and obliterated their wisdom, are unable to give rise to the roots of goodness (*kuśalamūla*) of the Mahāyāna.

The *Śūraṅgama Sūtra* asks: "What are the three characteristics of noble wisdom? They are: the characteristic of non-existence; the characteristic of the sphere of the spontaneous vows of all Buddhas; and self-awakening (*svasaṃvedana*)."

This is the characteristic of the ultimate realization of noble wisdom. Having attained this through practice, one is able to abandon the mental state and characteristics of the "crippled donkey" wisdom.

The commentary explains: "Crippled" means the feet are unable to walk; it carries the sense of being lame. This refers to the wisdom of the two vehicles (*śrāvaka* and *pratyekabuddha*), which functions only within emptiness.

Since emptiness and existence cannot function as a dual pair, it is taken as a metaphor. As for the "withered sprouts" and the "lame tortoises," they have not yet been seen recorded in the scriptures;
perhaps these are terms coined by the lecturer for the sake of pairing. This matter awaits further investigation.
"One cannot judge by words or appearance.

The Master said, "If one grants approval based solely on the earnestness of their discourse, it remains uncertain whether they are a true gentleman or merely someone putting on a formal countenance. The commentary states:
"This means that if one grants approval simply because their speech is earnest and substantial, it is not yet known whether they are a true gentleman or one who merely maintains a solemn expression."
Indeed. One cannot judge a person solely by their words or outward appearance; see the *Analects*, Part II.
"Knocking at the gate and striking the joints":

"knocking at the gate" refers to the crucial points that are difficult to pass through yet one manages to pass; "striking the joints" refers to the obstructed passages that are blocked yet one manages to penetrate.

This means striking its vital mechanism and hitting its essential joints. See the *Baohun yinyi* (Explanations of Sounds and Meanings of the Precious Instructions) and the *Shiyu* (Superfluous Appendices) in the *Shiji*.
Chen Zhen said to the Bearer of the Edict from Chu, Zhao Yang: "There was a man who gave a single cup of wine to the attendants of his residence. The attendants...
They said to one another, "Let us draw snakes on the ground; whoever finishes first shall drink. One man finished first and, raising his cup, said, "I can add feet to it.
As he was adding the feet, the other snatched the wine and drank, saying, "A snake has no feet.
Now that you have added feet, it is no longer a snake."
The Dragon Gate of the Leaping Cheeks is located on the western border of Hedong Commandery. This mountain rises five thousand *ren* (one *ren* equals eight feet) and has three tiers.
Its waters flow down below; every time the spring warmth arrives, vermilion carp gather at this mountain.

Descending, they swim upstream against the current. If there are those who possess the requisite fortune, they shall ascend and pass through the Dragon Gate. There, a celestial fire spontaneously burns their tails and sheds their scales;
they drive thunder and harness lightning, summoning clouds and bringing forth rain, thereby attaining transformation into dragons.

If they fail to ascend and pass through, they will have red vermilion dots on their foreheads and may not ascend again; they remain with gill-flaps exposed beneath the Dragon Gate. See the *Hui-xuan-ji*.
The *Zhongyong* states: "Today throughout the world, the chariots share the same ruts; the writings share the same characters; and conduct follows the same standards.
Zhang Juezheng’s commentary explains that Master Zisi’s intention was that although the present age is not the era of Kings Wen and Wu, its laws, systems, and statutes are nonetheless uniform.
From generation to generation they have been observed and followed; none have dared to differ or dissent. Let me illustrate this with three examples. Take a carriage:

though it is constructed by many individuals, the width of its ruts remains identical. Take written characters: though they are transcribed by many individuals, the forms of their strokes and components remain identical.
Take ritual propriety: though it is practiced by many individuals, the sequence of kinship—distant or near, noble or humble—remains identical.
There is no sequence that is not uniform; how much more so in the present age—how could one possibly go against it? To hold fast to this in one’s breast and never forget it, the Master said:
"The character of Hui was such that he chose from among the Mean; whenever he attained a single good point, he would grasp it firmly and hold it fast in his breast. And so forth.
"One does not lose it. The commentary states: Hui was a disciple of Confucius, surnamed Yan and styled Ziyuan. "Quanchuan" describes the manner of reverently upholding [the Way].
"Fu" means to wear; "ying" refers to the chest. To uphold and wear it within one's heart and chest means that one is able to maintain it.
This is seen in the *Zhongyong*.

When Tang was about to attack Jie, he followed the precedent of those who carried stones to sink in deep pools or threw themselves into boiling water, and he consulted Bian Sui regarding the plan. Bian Sui said, "This is not my business. Tang asked, "Who else would be suitable?"
He said, "I do not know. He then consulted with Mou Guang. Mou Guang said, "That is not my business. Tang asked, "Who would be suitable?
He replied, "I do not know. Tang asked, "What about Yi Yin? He replied, "He is strong-willed and endures indignity; I know nothing else of him.
Tang then followed Yi Yin's plan to attack Jie and conquered him. He then offered the throne to Bian Sui, but Bian Sui would not accept it.

He accepted [the throne], but then threw himself into the thick waters and died. He also yielded to Wuguang, who likewise did not accept it; he then carried a stone on his back and drowned himself in the Lu River.
This is recorded in the "Chapter on Yielding the Throne" (*Ràngwáng piān*) of the *Zhuāngzǐ*.
From the *Śūraṅgama Sūtra*, Fascicle Four.
The Buddha addressed Pūrṇa: "Although you have removed your doubts, other delusions remain unresolved.
I shall now question you again regarding various matters currently manifest in the world. Have you not heard of the city of Śrāvastī?"

If Sudatta were suddenly to look at his face in a mirror early in the morning and, loving the head in the mirror where the eyebrows and eyes are visible, yet hating his own head for not seeing its own features, were to think it was a malevolent spirit (*chīmèi*) and run about wildly and without cause—what do you think?
For what reason would this person run about wildly and without cause? Pūrṇa replied: "This person’s mind is deranged; there is no other cause. The Buddha said: "So it is."
It is said that they are like *chimei* (goblins) and other such spirits who fear themselves for having no heads; these are people whose minds have gone mad, having lost their original nature.
The ancient scriptures are likewise so.
Since antiquity, the scriptures have been bound in scrolls (*juan*). *Bitan* states that printed books did not yet exist at the beginning of the Tang dynasty;
their creation began with Feng Dao.

During the Wei and Zhou dynasties, the scriptures were burned and destroyed. When Emperor Shizu of the Yuan-Wei dynasty first ascended the throne, he followed the legacy of his Grandfather (Taizu) and frequently invited monks of high virtue to engage in discussion with him.
Cui Hao, the Minister of Education, was particularly distrustful of Buddhism; he would constantly inquire about state affairs and always harbor such thoughts in his mind, saying:
"Buddhism is empty and extravagant; it is a waste and a harm to the common people. The Way of the Yellow Emperor and Laozi can serve as a basis for the mind.
Later, when Gai Wu returned to Xingcheng, the Emperor launched a western campaign. Hao accompanied him there. Upon reaching Chang'an, an official entered a monk's quarters.
He saw a bow and arrows there and brought them out to report to the Emperor. The Emperor said in anger, "These are not things used by śramaṇas;
they must have conspired with Gaiwu to plot the harm of others. He ordered the authorities to investigate and execute the entire monastery, issuing an edict that stated:
"From the princes and dukes downward, anyone who privately maintains śramaṇas shall have their entire family exterminated. At that time, Prince Gongzong was the Crown Prince; every time he...
He submitted a memorial offering remonstrance, but the Emperor refused it in both instances. Hao again slandered him repeatedly, and the Emperor, believing his words, issued another edict stating:
"All shall be swept away. All images and foreign scriptures are to be smashed and burned. As for the śramaṇas, regardless of their age..."

He had them all slaughtered in a pit. Emperor Gaozu of the Northern Zhou was patient with resentment and harbored no ill will; he placed his trust in the *chan* (prophetic texts) and *wei* (astronomical commentaries), making them his sole guide.
According to ancient tradition, "black" signifies success; it was said that one possessing a black destiny would obtain the empire. For this reason, his clothing, vessels, and banners were all black.

They all turned black. At first, the Emperor held the Buddha-dharma in high esteem and would prostrate himself before śramaṇas. However, there was a Daoist named Zhang Bin, who was deceitful and sought to deceive the sovereign.
He privately instigated his own faction, claiming that the "black" Buddhists were a national calamity while the "yellow" followers of Laozi were a national blessing.

The Emperor accepted these words; he came to trust the Dao and look down upon the Buddha. At that time, there was a monk named Wei Yuansong, who joined forces with Zhang Bin like lips and teeth, fanning their mutual influence to delude and agitate the Emperor.

The Emperor subsequently summoned virtuous monks, renowned scholars, and eminent Daoist masters to convene three rounds of deliberations. As the debates on right and wrong became increasingly extensive, none could satisfy the Emperor’s mind.
Thus, five years passed until the third year of the Jiande era, when he issued an edict commanding both monks and Daoists to return to secular life.

The wealth and property belonging to the Triple Gem were distributed among his ministers, while temples, monasteries, stupas, and shrines were granted to the princes and dukes; consequently, even the scriptures were affected by this.
[The temples were] destroyed. For details on these two matters, see the *Guang hongming ji* (Extended Collection for Propagating and Clarifying [Buddhism]).

Regarding the verse from the *Ji ji duo shi* (The Multitude of Talented Men): "In the kingdom he was born; he was the integrity of Zhou. A multitude of talented men; because of them, King Wen found peace. The commentary states: [...]

"Zhen" (zhēn) means the sturdy trunk. "Jijì" (jǐjǐ) signifies a multitude of forms. This refers to how the state of King Wen was able to produce such a great number of scholars that they were sufficient to serve as the backbone of the nation, and King Wen likewise relied upon them for his security. This is seen in the "King Wen" chapter of the *Dàyā*.

The *Bianxun tiannü huayan jing* (The Flower Adornment Sutra on the Goddess Bianxun), Fascicle Twenty-nine, states: "Furthermore, O Son of the Buddha, it is like the Heavenly King Vaśavartin, who has a celestial maiden named Śubhavaktrā.
From within her mouth, she emits a single sound, and that sound [resonates] with hundreds of thousands..."
Various musical instruments were played in harmonious concert. Within each single instrument, there were further hundreds of thousands of distinct sounds.
O Son of the Buddha, from a single voice from the mouth of that woman of virtuous speech, such immeasurable sounds issued forth.
△ Volume One, Part One (Upper).

"The people are rarely able to abide in it for long," said the Master. "The Doctrine of the Mean—how supreme it is! The people are rarely able to abide in it for long. The commentary states: "To exceed it is to lose the Mean. Not...
When one reaches it, one has not yet arrived; therefore, only the virtue of the Mean (zhōngyōng) is ultimate. Yet this is something all people are equally capable of attaining.
However, because the teachings of the world have declined and the people do not promote virtuous conduct, few are able to achieve it. This has long been the case. To see the Mean—this is rare indeed.
According to the *Zhou Li*, each of the four quarters had its own officials in charge of their respective languages.
The "Wangzhi" chapter of the *Liji* states: "The people of the five regions have languages that do not communicate with one another and desires that differ from one another.

To convey their intentions and facilitate their needs: those of the east are called *ji*; those of the south are called *xiang*; those of the west are called *didi*; and those of the north are called..."

Translation: Fang [Yun] said: "Ji" (to lodge) means that one can lodge within this [land] the differences of its customs; "xiang" (to resemble) means that one can imitate and resemble the differences of the customs there;
"di" (shoes) is intended to distinguish the differences in their clothing and ornaments; and "yi" (to interpret) is intended to discern the differences in their languages.
Mencius said: "I have not been able to become a disciple of Confucius; I have privately cultivated my virtue through others. The commentary states: "Privately" (si) means "stealthily" (qie).
"Cultivated" (shu) means "good" (shan). "Others" refers to the disciples of Zisi. This means that although I have not received [his teachings] directly...
Yue was at the gate of Confucius. Yet, the influence of the Sage still remained, and there were still those capable of transmitting his teachings.
Thus, I was able to hear the Way of Confucius from others and privately apply it to cultivate myself.
This is likely a humble expression used to extol Confucius while modestly disparaging oneself; see the "Li Lou" chapter.
In ancient times, Duke Huan of Qi was reading a book in his hall. Wheelwright Lün Bian was planing wheels below the hall.
Setting aside his hammer and chisel, he ascended the steps and addressed Duke Huan, saying, "May I venture to ask what it is that Your Highness is reading? The Duke replied, "The words of the sages."
[The King] said, "Is there perhaps a sage among us? Gong replied, "There is none. [Qian] Bian said, "In that case, what Your Majesty reads is merely the dregs of the ancients.
Gong said, "When I read books, how can a wheelwright dare to criticize them? If you have an argument, it may be permitted;
if you have no argument, you shall die. Bian said, "Judging from my own craft: if [the spokes] are too slow, they will be sweet-sounding but not firm; if they are too fast..."
Thus, it was painful and he could not enter [the state of mastery]. Neither too slow nor too fast, he attained it in his heart and responded with his hand;
his mouth could not describe it, for a certain measure existed within that interval. The master could not explain it to his son, and the son likewise could not receive it from the master.
For this reason, he reached the age of seventy and grew old at his wheelwright’s bench. Such was the man of antiquity. And so it is with him.
That which cannot be transmitted is dead. Thus, what you, sir, read is but the dregs of the ancients. As the *Jingjie* (Essential Explanations) says:
"One who feeds on dregs and lees—how could they know the flavor of wine? One who reads the bequeathed books of the ancients—how could they know the flavor of the Way?
This is seen in the "Heavenly Way" (*Tian Dao*) chapter of the *Zhuangzi*.
The Buddha manifested ten kinds of supernatural transformations to deliver them:

namely, that the venomous dragon could not harm him; the dragon’s fire could not burn him; the waters of the Ganges could not drown him; he took fruit from the three directions and non-glutinous rice from the north; he took ambrosia from the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven;
he vanished when he knew they were weary of him and appeared again when he knew they were mindful of him; and the extinguished fire was made to blaze up once more.

The axe was raised but would not descend; this is seen in detail in the *Ruiying jing* (Sūtra on Auspicious Responses) and in the *Pravrajyā-vastu* (Chapter on Receiving the Precepts) of the various Vinayas.

The sixth fascicle of the *Bao'en jing* (Sūtra on Repaying Kindness), concerning Jīvaka’s chariot, states: "Maudgalyāyana, because of a disciple's illness, ascended to the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven to inquire with Jīvaka."
Just as the various devas were entering the Garden of Joy (Nandana), Maudgalyāyana was standing by the side of the road.
None of the devas looked back at him. Jīvaka arrived later; seeing Maudgalyāyana, he raised one hand toward him and drove his carriage straight past.

Maudgalyāyana thought to himself, "This person was formerly my disciple in the human realm; now, having received celestial blessings, he has become so attached to heavenly pleasures that he has completely lost his original resolve.
He then used his supernormal powers to restrain the chariot and bring it to a halt. Jīvaka descended from the chariot and prostrated at Maudgalyāyana’s feet.
Maudgalyāyana rebuked him for his impropriety through various causes and conditions.
Jīvaka said, "Because I am a disciple of a Great Virtuous One among men, I raise my hand to inquire after his health. Have you ever seen the devas act in such a manner?
It is because the devas are deeply attached to pleasure and lack self-mastery that they act thus. Maudgalyāyana asked, "When a disciple is ill, one ought—"
"How is he to be treated? Jīvaka replied, "Fasting is the primary treatment.
Once Śakra had defeated the asuras in battle, he built the Vaijayanta Palace, which was adorned with extraordinary beauty. Maudgalyāyana went there to see it.

The celestial maidens all hid themselves away and did not emerge. Maudgalyāyana, mindful that Śakra was attached to pleasure and failed to cultivate the foundation of the Path, used his supernormal powers to incinerate his palace.
He then preached the Dharma of impermanence, suffering, and emptiness to Śakra. Śakra rejoiced;
yet afterwards, the palace remained as it was, without a trace of ash or smoke. This is recorded in the *Fahua Wenju* (Explanatory Text on the Lotus Sutra).
The *Pañcavargika-vinaya*, chapter twenty-five, states:

At that time, Devadatta established five propositions for himself and led five hundred newly ordained bhikṣus to perform the *poṣadha* ceremony together as a unified assembly. Then Śāriputra and Maudgalyāyana went to that group. Devadatta...
He then said, "Welcome! You may take this seat. Previously you were the foremost disciples of the śramaṇa Gautama;
now you shall again be my foremost disciples—is this not excellent? Śāriputra and Maudgalyāyana remained silent and did not answer.
Devadatta, assuming they had accepted his words, immediately followed the Buddha’s customary practice and addressed them, saying, "You two shall preach the Dharma to the assembly; I..."
"My back aches slightly; you should take care of yourself. He then folded his saṃghāṭī robe fourfold and lay down on his right side.
Because he was not maintaining mindfulness, he soon fell into a deep sleep and turned onto his left side, snoring so loudly as to startle people.
At that time, Maudgalyāyana manifested various supernatural transformations, and Śāriputra preached various sublime Dharmas. Having seen and heard this, five hundred bhikṣus immediately—
Seated upon it, he was distanced from dust and freed from defilement; regarding all phenomena, he attained the pure Dharma-eye.

He took a member of the Śākya clan to hide him from the Brahmā-deva King Prasenajit’s son, named Devadatta. Because Devadatta had playfully sat upon the Buddha’s seat, he incurred censure and formed a grudge, later desiring—
He raised an army and went to wage war against the Śākyas. Maudgalyāyana addressed the Buddha, saying, "Devadatta is going to wage war against the Śākyas;

I wish to move their four assemblies and cast them into other directions. The Buddha said, "Though you possess wisdom and virtue, you will ultimately be unable to establish peace. Maudgalyāyana’s resolve did not cease;
he then took four or five thousand of his acquaintances, placed them all within his almsbowl, and lifted them up to place them in the Brahma Heaven. [The army...]

After the soldiers had departed, Maudgalyāyana addressed the Buddha, saying, "Relying upon the Buddha’s spiritual power, I have rescued four or five thousand people. The Buddha said, "Go and look at them.
When Maudgalyāyana lowered his alms bowl, he saw that all were already dead. This is detailed in the *Commentary on the Yuanjue Jing* (Yuanjue shuchao).

The *Record of the Essentials of the Tathāgata’s Defeat* states: When the Brahmin Akṣapāda established his doctrine, he made a pact with the Buddha, saying, "If my doctrine falls, I shall cut off my own head. The Buddha asked, "What do you take as your fundamental tenet? He replied, "I accept nothing at all. The Buddha then asked, "Do you accept this? [He replied,] "No. The Buddha said, "Since you do not accept even this, why do you claim that you accept nothing? Thereupon, the Brahmin was defeated; he took up a sword and struck at his own neck, but the Buddha’s supernatural power protected him, and he did not die. The Buddha then preached the Dharma to him, and he subsequently attained the fruit of Arhatship. It is for this reason that it is called "the defeat of Akṣapāda. Furthermore, the *Mahāyāna-saṃparigraha-śāstra* says: "The Brahmin Akṣapāda, having been defeated by the Buddha, struck his own neck with a sword, but the Buddha’s supernatural power protected him so that he did not die. This is what is meant by "Akṣapāda striking his own neck. Regarding the phrase "the Brahmin Akṣapāda": "Akṣapāda" means "footless"; it refers to one who has no feet. Because he had no feet, he could not travel far, and thus he remained in one place. Therefore, he is called "Akṣapāda. Regarding the phrase "establishing his doctrine": "doctrine" refers to the principles of the teachings. To "establish" them means to set them forth and explain them. Regarding the phrase "made a pact with the Buddha": "pact" refers to a formal agreement. To "make a pact" means to establish a covenant. Regarding the phrase "if my doctrine falls": "doctrine" refers to the principles of the teachings. To "fall" means to be defeated or overturned. Regarding the phrase "I shall cut off my own head": "head" refers to the crown of the skull. To "cut off" means to sever. Regarding the phrase "what do you take as your fundamental tenet?": "tenet" refers to the core principle of a doctrine. To "take as a tenet" means to accept and uphold it. Regarding the phrase "I accept nothing at all": "nothing" refers to the absence of any object. To "accept" means to acknowledge. Regarding the phrase "do you accept this?": "this" refers to the aforementioned statement. To "accept" means to acknowledge. Regarding the phrase "since you do not accept even this": "even this" refers to the aforementioned statement. To "not accept" means to not acknowledge. Regarding the phrase "why do you claim that you accept nothing?": "claim" means to state. To "accept nothing" means to have no position whatsoever. Regarding the phrase "thereupon the Brahmin was defeated": "defeated" means to be overturned. Regarding the phrase "he took up a sword and struck at his own neck": "sword" refers to a blade weapon. To "strike" means to hit. Regarding the phrase "the Buddha’s supernatural power protected him": "supernatural power" refers to the Buddha’s spiritual efficacy. To "protect" means to guard. Regarding the phrase "he did not die": "die" means to perish. Regarding the phrase "the Buddha then preached the Dharma to him": "preach" means to expound. Regarding the phrase "he subsequently attained the fruit of Arhatship": "fruit" refers to the result of practice. To "attain" means to realize. Regarding the phrase "it is for this reason that it is called 'the defeat of Akṣapāda'": "for this reason" means because of these causes and conditions. To "call" means to name. Regarding the phrase "furthermore, the *Mahāyāna-saṃparigraha-śāstra* says": "furthermore" indicates an additional point. To "say" means to record. Regarding the phrase "the Brahmin Akṣapāda, having been defeated by the Buddha": "having been defeated" means having been overturned. Regarding the phrase "struck his own neck with a sword": "neck" refers to the nape of the neck. To "strike" means to hit. Regarding the phrase "the Buddha’s supernatural power protected him": "protected" means to guard. Regarding the phrase "so that he did not die": "did not die" means he did not perish. Regarding the phrase "this is what is meant by 'Akṣapāda striking his own neck'": "this is what is meant" means this is the intended meaning. Regarding the phrase "regarding the phrase 'the Brahmin Akṣapāda'": "regarding" means concerning. Regarding the phrase "Akṣapāda means 'footless'": "means" indicates an explanation. Regarding the phrase "it refers to one who has no feet": "refers to" means it denotes.
