"Did you see? Zhi shook his sleeves and departed. Reaching the middle of the road, he suddenly attained realization and sighed, saying:

"In both instances I have fallen into error. When I saw that [the master] accepted it, my failure was coarse; when I saw that he did not accept it, my failure was subtle. I do not understand this principle at all;
only the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas know where my conceptual fallacy lies. I shall cut off my own head to apologize to the Buddha. He returned to the Buddha’s presence.
He addressed the Buddha, saying, "World-Honored One, I have been defeated and fallen in two matters regarding my own doctrine. I now beg for my head to be cut off as an apology to the Buddha.

The Buddha said, "In my Dharma, there is no such thing. You should turn your mind toward the Path. Thereupon, together with his five hundred followers, he threw himself before the Buddha to leave the household life and attained the fruit of Arhatship.
The Buddha said, "Rāhula, in a past life, you were once a king. At that time, there was a rishi who came and spoke to the king."
"The king’s law punishes thieves; you ought to be punished for your crime. The king asked, "What crime have you committed?

The seer replied, "I entered your kingdom and committed the offense of taking what was not given, using your water and your tooth-sticks. The king said, "I have bestowed my water and tooth-sticks upon all beings;
what crime could there be in this? The seer replied, "Though it be so, O King, my mind is filled with doubt and regret that can never be dispelled."
The king said, "If you must have it so, wait a short while until I have entered and returned. The king entered the palace and did not emerge for six days.
While the seer remained in the king's garden, he suffered from hunger and thirst for six days and thought to himself, "The king is surely punishing me for this."
After six days had passed, the king took his leave of the rishi, saying, "I have forgotten you; do not hold me in blame.
Because of these causes and conditions, he underwent the suffering of the three evil realms for five hundred lifetimes. For five hundred lifetimes, he remained in his mother’s womb for six years.
This is detailed in the seventeenth fascicle of the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra*.
The *Qu li* (Ceremonial Etiquette) of the *Li ji* states: "When asked about the age of the Son of Heaven, one replies: 'I have heard that he has recently donned robes of such-and-such length.
The commentary notes: "If" (*ruo*) means "like" (*ru*). It is an indefinite term. Numbers begin with one and are completed by ten; the character for "ten" (*gan*)...
It is derived from "one" and "ten," hence it is called "several" (若干). This means that whether it be like one or like ten—indeed, any number that is not yet fixed may be so described.
Ānanda made three requests on her behalf.
At that time, the World-Honored One was in the Nyagrodha Park. Mahāprajāpatī, together with five hundred Śākya women, went to where the Buddha was, prostrated at his feet, and said:
"World-Honored One, we pray that you will grant permission for women [to enter the order] under the Buddha..."
"Among the Dharma, one leaves the household life to practice the Way. The Buddha said, "Stop, Mahāprajāpatī Gautamī! Do not speak such words.
I do not yet wish for women to leave the household life to practice the Way within the Buddha-dharma. The Buddha returned to Śrāvastī.
Mahāprajāpatī and the others shaved their own heads, donned the saṃghāṭī robes, and went to stand outside the gate of Jetavana. Their feet were broken by the walking, and they shed tears.
She wept with flowing tears. Having seen this, Ānanda questioned her and learned the reason; he immediately went to inform the Buddha: "Excellent, World-Honored One!
We pray that you will allow women to leave the household life and receive the precepts within the Buddha-dharma. The Buddha told Ānanda: "Stop!
Do not desire that women leave the household life and receive the precepts within the Buddha-dharma. Why is this? If women [were to enter] within the Buddha-dharma..."
"If women go forth from home and receive the precepts, it will cause the Buddha-dharma not to endure for long.

Ānanda said to the Buddha, "If women are permitted to go forth and receive the precepts, would they be able to attain the fruit of Arhatship? The Buddha replied, "They can attain it. [Ānanda said,] "If they can attain the fruit, I pray that the Buddha will grant permission.
The Buddha told Ānanda, "I shall now establish for women eight rules to be observed for as long as life lasts, which must not be transgressed."
If one is able to practice this, it constitutes the reception of the precepts; see in detail the forty-eighth fascicle of the *Dharmaguptaka-vinaya*.

Regarding the stages of non-retrogression and so forth, the Tiantai school states that there are three types of delusions: namely, those of views (*dṛṣṭi*), of thought (*saṃjñā*), and of dust-sands (*rajas*) and ignorance (*avidyā*). If one destroys the delusions of views and thought, one realizes emptiness (*śūnyatā*).
The principle of tranquility is called "non-retrogression from rank," because one never loses the supramundane position.
If one cuts through the sands of afflictions and is able to practice the path of transformation, it is called "non-retrogression from conduct," because one never loses the bodhisattva practices.
If one destroys ignorance and personally realizes the dharma-nature, it is called "non-retrogression from mindfulness," because one never loses the correct mindfulness of the Middle Way.

In his courtyard, the eight *yi* were arrayed; Confucius spoke thus regarding the House of Ji. "The House of Ji performed the dance of the eight *yi* in their courtyard. The commentary states: "The House of Ji refers to the Great Officer of Lu, the clan of Jisun.
*Yi* refers to the rows of dancers. The Son of Heaven employs eight [rows], the feudal lords six, the great officers four, and the scholars two. The number of persons in each *yi* is as follows:"
The number of rows [of the retinue] is as seen in the *Analects*, Part One.

The *Mahā-amitābha-sūtra* (Da-mi-tuo jing), concerning the transformation of Amitābha’s countenance, states: "One day, the World-Honored One’s facial expression was extraordinary. Ānanda asked, 'Since I have served [the Buddha],'"

"Buddha, I have never before beheld your majestic countenance as I do today. Is it not because you are mindful of the Buddhas of the past, or mindful of the Buddhas of the future, that this has come to pass?
The commentary states: This concerns Ānanda’s inquiry regarding the transformation of the World-Honored One’s physical appearance.
It was for this reason that the Tathāgata praised his question and spoke [the discourse]; this constitutes the introduction to the sutra.
Regarding the "Lengyan [Sutra] on Falling into Lust," the *Śūraṅgama Sūtra* states: At that time, Ānanda, while on his almsround, passed by a brothel and encountered a great illusionist.
The Mātangī girl, using the *sāvikāra-pūrvabrahmamantra*, drew him into her bedchamber for sexual purposes; she touched his body with her own, nearly destroying his precept-body.
The commentary states: This refers to the incident where Ānanda mistakenly fell into the lecher’s chamber. Because of this, the Tathāgata...
The Buddha of Transformed Light atop the crown of the head spoke a mantra; Mañjuśrī took the mantra and went to provide protection.
When Ānanda returned, he piteously entreated for the wondrous samādhi, and the Tathāgata accordingly revealed it to him in successive stages; thus, this serves as the introductory narrative.

When the disciples were indignant and perplexed, the Master said: "I do not reveal [the truth] until they are indignant; I do not expound it until they are perplexed. The commentary states: "Indignation" refers to the state of the mind seeking understanding but not yet having attained it;
"perplexity" refers to the appearance of the mouth wishing to speak but being unable to do so. "Revealing" means opening up their understanding; "expounding" means bringing it to completion.
The wording [of this passage] is found in the *Analects*, Volume One.
It is like the metaphor of "ten thousand streams flowing toward the source," as previously cited in the section on "When Water Reaches Its End, All Flow Toward the Source."

"The multitude of stars revolve around the North Star," the Master said. "To govern by means of virtue is like the North Star, which remains in its place while the multitude of stars revolve around it. The commentary states:
"The term 'governance' (*zheng*) signifies 'rectification. It is that by which one rectifies the incorrectness of others. The term 'virtue' (*de*) signifies 'attainment.'"

This means that through the practice of the Way, one attains realization within the mind. The Northern Star (Beichen), the North Pole (Beiji), is the pivot of Heaven. It remains in its place without moving;
this describes how the myriad stars revolve around it from all four directions while converging toward it. This is seen in the *Analects*, Part I.
Regarding the ritual of the *huáng* (reed organ), the *Lùmíng* chapter of the *Xiǎoyǎ* of the *Shī* states: "I have a distinguished guest; they play the *qín* and blow the *shēng*.

They blow the *shēng* and strike the *huáng*, while presenting gifts within a basket. The commentary notes: "The *huáng* refers to the reeds within the *shēng*. A large *shēng* has nineteen reeds; a small *shēng* has ten."
The *sāṅ* (three-reed instrument) was created by the Lord Nüwa. A *huáng* (reed) is the thin gold leaf within a *shēng* (mouth-organ).
Generally, both the *shēng* and the *yú* (ancient reed organ) consist of bamboo tubes set vertically within a gourd; the sides of the tube bases are perforated and covered with thin gold leaf.
When blown upon, these are struck to produce sound—this is what is meant by "beating the reeds" (*gǔ huáng*). Now, Maitreya manifests as if unaware, yet he moves and stirs Mañjuśrī.
This serves as the opening for the exposition of the Dharma; it is somewhat analogous to this.
As Mencius said: "A person constantly errs, and only then can they reform. When the mind is distressed and anxieties are rampant, only then does one act. (Commentary)
"Yún" (云) means "constantly. It is also used to mean "generally" or "for the most part. "Hèng" (橫) means "not in accord with" or "unfavorable. "Zuò" (作) means "to rouse oneself" or "to exert effort.
This passage states that the nature of ordinary people must always involve transgressions before they can reform.

Because they are unable to exercise caution in their daily lives, it is only when circumstances become desperate and extreme—leading to a state where the mind is distressed and anxieties are turbulent—that they are finally able to rouse themselves and achieve self-improvement. This is seen in the *Mencius*.
The following is from the "Chapter on Instructing the Sons" (*Xiagao zizi pian*).

Regarding the closing of the gates to sight and hearing at the sublime assembly, the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra*, in the "Entering the Dharma Realm" (*Rufajie pin*) chapter, states: "At that time, the foremost great śrāvakas—Śāriputra, and so forth..."
As for Pūrṇa and the others who were in the Jeta Grove, they all failed to perceive the Tathāgata’s supernatural powers or his physical marks and signs (*lakṣaṇa-vyañjana*).
They did not even perceive the inconceivable realm of the bodhisattvas. The *Qīngliáng xù* (Preface to the *Qīngliáng*) states:
"The śrāvakas of superior virtue closed their sight and hearing at this auspicious assembly. Here, "superior virtue" refers to the leaders; "closed" means to have blocked them. They were [there].
"Seeing" refers to the eyes; "hearing" refers to the ears. "Auspicious assembly" (*jiahui*) specifically indicates the Śītavana Grove.

It means that when the Tathāgata entered the Lion’s Stretching Samādhi within the Jeta Grove and manifested the inconceivable realm of the Bodhisattvas, the Śrāvakas sitting in the assembly were as if blind and deaf;
hence it is said that their sight and hearing were obstructed.
When the Good Friend entered the sea, he sought this very thing.
The *Bao'en jing* (Sūtra on Requiting Kindness) states: In a past age, there was a king named Mahārāja who had two sons.
The first was named Good Friend (Kalyāṇamitra), and the second was named Evil Friend (Pāpamitra). Prince Good Friend was dearly loved by his parents.

One day, while out on an excursion, he saw many people suffering in distress. He petitioned his father to provide relief for them; before long, two-thirds of the goods within the treasury had been spent.
The Good Friend, unable to bear depleting the treasuries of his parents, entered the great ocean and obtained from the left ear of a nāga king a wish-fulfilling maṇi jewel.
This jewel could rain down treasures at will, as well as all other necessary things, providing for sentient beings so that none lacked anything.
This is a brief citation according to the meaning; the details are as found in that sūtra.

Regarding the contemplation of one's wife and concubines as being like painted vases, the *Chuyao jing* (Sūtra of the Exalted Utterances) states: "Long ago, there was a man of licentious character whose mind was exclusively devoted to female beauty;
he could not separate himself from them. A learned practitioner who frequented his home spoke to his wife, saying: 'My husband is by nature full of lustful desire. I fear that...'"
He could not save himself. The practitioner said, "When your husband approaches you, tell him: 'Is it according to the principle of the Srotāpanna-dharma that one should act thus?
Later, she indeed spoke to him as instructed. Her husband felt profound shame and from then on forever ceased his lustful activities.
His wife asked, "For what reason have you forever ceased your lustful activities? Her husband then painted a beautiful jar and filled it with excrement.
[He] defiled it and sealed its mouth. He ordered his wife to embrace it as if it were no different from himself. The wife followed his words and held the jar without letting go.
Her husband then took the jar and broke it, saying: "I observe your body; it is even more loathsome than this jar, from head to foot."
There are thirty-six constituent parts that are filthy and impure; what is there to crave?
When Zengzi was ill, he summoned his disciples and said, "Uncover my feet; uncover my hands. The commentary states: "Uncover" (*qǐ*) means to open.
Zengzi had always maintained that since his body was received from his parents, he did not dare to damage or injure it;
therefore, he had his disciples pull back his shroud and examine it. This is recorded in the *Analects*, Part One.

"To sacrifice one's life to fulfill what is right," the Master said. "The man of resolve and the man of benevolence do not seek to preserve their lives at the expense of harming their benevolence; rather, they are those who would sacrifice their lives to fulfill their benevolence.
The commentary states: "The man of resolve is one who possesses a firm will; the man of benevolence is one who has perfected his virtue. When the principle dictates death, yet one seeks to live..."
Then there will be unease in one's mind; this harms the virtue of the mind. To die when it is time to die results in a peaceful mind and the perfection of virtue. See the Analects, Part II.
Bi Gan剖 (pòu) 腹 (fù) 比干 (Bǐ Gān).
He was the paternal uncle of Zhòu. Zhòu obtained a woman from the Sū clan named Dàjī; he doted on her greatly.
He established a wine-pool and a forest of meat, ordering men and women to strip naked and chase one another therein. He constructed the Chángyè Palace, which measured one hundred and ten [units].

One day constituted a single solar cycle. He employed the "burning pillar" (páo luò) execution; he disemboweled pregnant women and castrated young men. He constructed the Lùtái Terrace, which was completed only after seven years.

He cruelly oppressed and harmed loyal and virtuous ministers. His minister, Shù Bìgān, exhausted his loyalty in offering remonstrance, but [the King] would not listen; he subsequently had his heart cut out and died. This is recorded in the *Bǎoxùn bǐshuō*.

Regarding the realm of all lands, a poem says: "Under the vast heavens, there are none that are not the King’s soil; along the shores of all lands, there are none who are not the King’s subjects. The commentary states:

*Pu* (溥) is synonymous with *pu* (普), meaning "universal" or "pervasive. *Shuai* (率) means "to follow" or "to govern. *Bin* (濱) refers to the "margins" or "borders. The statement means: "Under the entire sky, there is no land that is not the King's territory;
among those dwelling on the borders of all lands, there is no one who is not the King's subject. This is explained in detail in the "Beishan" (North Mountain) chapter of the *Xiaoya* (Minor Odes).
"Regarding the world as if it were a worn-out sandal," says Mencius.
"Shun regarded the abandonment of the empire as if he were casting off a worn-out sandal. The commentary states: "A *xiè* (sandal) is a straw shoe; *bì* (worn-out) means ruined or broken.
This is said to express how lightly he viewed the empire. See the *Jinxin Pian* (Chapter on the Exhaustion of the Mind) in the lower part of the *Mencius*.

Regarding the passage where Confucius answers Fan Chi’s question on distinguishing delusion, it says: "To forget one's own person and one's parents out of a single moment of anger—is this not delusion?
The commentary states: "One knows that a single moment of anger is a very minor matter, yet the resulting calamity reaches one's parents; [this is why it is called delusion]."
"Great! This provides a means to discern delusion and restrain one's anger. See the *Analects*, Part II.
Regarding dwelling among trees and stones and roaming with deer and pigs, *Mencius* says:
"When Shun lived in the midst of the deep mountains, he dwelt among trees and stones and roamed with deer and pigs. As for what he... [text fragment ends]
He differs from the common people of the deep mountains and wilds by only a very small degree. See the "Jinxin" (Exerting the Mind) chapter of the *Mengzi*.

Regarding the passage where [the disciples] ate parched grain and ate herbs, the *Mengzi* says: "When Shun ate parched grain and ate herbs, it was as if he would do so for the rest of his life. The commentary states: "Fàn" means to eat.
"Qiù" refers to dried provisions; "rú" also means food. This expresses that the mind of the Sage does not harbor longings for external things because of poverty or low status.
See the "Jìn Xīn Piān" (Chapter on the Exhaustion of the Mind) in the lower part of the *Mèngzi*.
The *Zhongyong* says: "To hit the mark without striving and to attain it without thinking—this is sincerity (*cheng*). Sincerity is the Way of Heaven; that which seeks sincerity is the Way of man.

One who possesses sincerity hits the mark without striving and attains it without thinking, moving with ease within the Middle Way; such is the Sage. As for one who seeks sincerity, they choose what is good and make it firm."
This refers to those who grasp [the meaning].

Regarding the different forms of *bǐ* (comparison) and *xìng* (evocation), the commentary on the *Shijing* states: "Comparison (*bǐ*) is metaphorical illustration. Since it is not easily understood to speak of a single object alone, one takes another [object] as a counterpart."
A "parallel" (pi) refers to taking one object and comparing it to another, so that a person may understand this [subject] by means of that [object].
An "exordium" (xing) means "arising. When one wishes to compose a verse, one first mentions another object to give rise to the expression.
The *Cān-lín Bǎo-xùn* (Precious Instructions of the Zen Forest) states: "In the transmission between former sages, it was certainly not something that those of shallow capacity dared to uphold;
only when it is like water poured from one vessel into another can one truly succeed to the grand regulations."

Regarding "Vigilant and Tranquil," the *Wenyang ji* (Collection of Yongjia) states: "Vigilant and tranquil—this is correct; merely tranquil and lacking awareness—this is not. Tranquil and vigilant—this is correct;
discursive thoughts and vigilance—this is not. The commentary explains: "Wisdom is all-pervasive and constantly still; function arises in profusion yet remains eternally as-it-is. This is called...
Vigilant stillness: if it were a state of indeterminate stillness, one would fall into a dull stagnation; therefore, it is not that.

To manifest all modes of conduct without arising from the samādhi of cessation—this is called "stillness within vigilance. If it were a vigilance of distracted thoughts, one would fall into discursive preoccupation; therefore, it is not that.

Regarding the passage, "Śūnyatā-janman sat in meditative seclusion while Śakra scattered flowers," the *Miyituo Yanyi* (Commentary on Amitābha) states: "Śūnyatā-janman was sitting in meditative seclusion within a stone chamber. Śakra, from the midst of the sky, scattered flowers as an offering.
Śūnyatā-janman asked, 'Who is it that scatters these flowers? He replied, 'It is Śakra, the Lord of Devas. [Śūnyatā-janman] asked, 'For what purpose? He replied, 'Because..."
The Venerable One spoke well of Prajñāpāramitā. The Venerable One said, "I have originally said nothing. Śakra said, "I likewise have heard nothing.
To have neither spoken nor heard is indeed true speaking and true hearing.

In the forty-eighth fascicle of the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra*, it is said that those in hell who receive this light suddenly transcend the stages of the ten bhūmis. The Buddha addressed the Bodhisattva Ratnapāṇi, saying:

"O Son of the Buddha, on the soles of the Bodhisattva’s feet there is the mark of a thousand-spoked wheel named King Universal Radiance. There is also a secondary mark (anuvyañjana) named King Perfection, which is constantly..."
He emitted forty kinds of light rays. Among them was one ray named "Pure Merit," which could illuminate worlds as numerous as the atoms within a hundred million nayutas of Buddha-fields.
According to the various karmic actions and diverse inclinations of sentient beings, it caused them all to reach maturity.
When those in the Avīci Hell who suffer extreme agony encountered this light, they all passed away and were reborn.
In the Tuṣita Heaven, once they had been born there, the celestial drum resounded and extensively preached the Dharma, even saying:
"At that time, the sons of heaven, having heard the exposition of the vast and extensive dedication of Samantabhadra, attained the fruit of the ten stages."
The Story of the Grass-Tied Goose-Necklace:
Once there was a bhikṣu who was plundered by bandits. Fearing that he would report them to the village, one of the men, knowing that the bhikṣu protected living beings, bound him with fresh grass.
The bhikṣu, fearing he might harm the life of the grass, did not dare to move. Later...
There was a king who, while out hunting, saw [the bhikṣu] and questioned him. The bhikṣu fully explained the reason for his presence.
The king untied the grass for the bhikṣu and departed. (See *Mahāvyūha-śāstra*, fascicle three). Formerly, there was a mendicant bhikṣu who went to the house of a jeweler.
It happened that he encountered the craftsman working for the king, stringing pearls. Seeing the bhikṣu arrive, [the craftsman] rejoiced and, taking the alms bowl, entered the house to fetch [food].
While he was eating, a goose swallowed a pearl. A bhikṣu saw it; fearing that he might harm the goose’s life, he remained silent because of this.
When the jeweler saw that his pearls were few, he suspected the bhikṣu of theft and proceeded to beat him. Blood flowed from every wound.

The goose came to peck at the blood, and the man, filled with rage, struck the goose with a staff until it died. Having seen this, the bhikṣu finally spoke the truth. The man then cut [the goose] open.
The goose obtained the pearl; filled with shame and remorse, it apologized for its offense. This is seen in the eleventh fascicle of the *Mahāvyūha-śāstra* (*Dà zhuāngyán lùn*).
Yan Yuan looked up and sighed, saying: "The more I look up, the higher it seems; the more I drill into it, the harder it becomes. I gaze for it to be before me, and suddenly—"
[The Master] was behind him. The commentary states: "Què" is a sound of deep sighing. [Yan Yuan said: "The higher I look up, the more remote he becomes; the deeper I drill, the more solid he proves.

Whether before or behind, he is elusive and cannot be defined by form. This was Yan Yuan’s profound realization that the Way of the Master is inexhaustible and lacks fixed boundaries or substance, and his expression of this through sighs. See the *Analects*, Part One.
"Severity and leniency should complement one another. When Zheng Zichan was ill, he said to Zitatu: "When I am dead, you must surely govern.
Only those possessed of virtue can subdue the people through leniency; next best is severity. Now, fire is fierce; when the people see it, they stand in awe, and thus few dare to approach it."

He died there. Because the water was shallow and sluggish, the people became familiar with it and treated it with casualness, resulting in many deaths. Thus, leniency is difficult to manage. Within a few months, [Zhongzi] passed away.

When Tai Shu took over the administration, he could not bear to be harsh and instead adopted a lenient policy. Consequently, banditry flourished in the state of Zheng; they seized people from the marshes of Huán and Fú.
Tai Shu regretted this, saying, "If I had followed the Master's advice earlier, I would not have come to this. He then raised a force of common soldiers...
To suppress the bandits of Huánfú, he slaughtered them all, and the banditry was somewhat quelled. Zhòngní said, "Excellent! When government is lenient, the people become arrogant;
when they are arrogant, one must restrain them with severity. When severity prevails, the people suffer injury; when they suffer injury, one must apply leniency.
Use leniency to complement severity, and severity to complement leniency; thus the administration will achieve harmony. This is recorded in the *Zuǒzhuan*.
"Rituals, music, and military expeditions must issue from the Son of Heaven.

in the first year of the Yanhe era of the Han dynasty, the Yuezhi kingdom of the Western Hu dispatched an envoy to present four *liang* of incense, each piece as large as a sparrow’s egg.
The color [of the incense] was like that of mulberry fruit. In the first year of the Shih (Shi) era, a great epidemic broke out in the capital, and more than half of the population died.

The Emperor took the incense and burned it; those who had been dead for less than three days all returned to life. The fragrance did not dissipate for three months. This incense originated from Mount Ren-ao on the island of Juku-zhou.
Its trees resemble maple trees, and its scent can be smelled for several li. It is called the "Soul-Returning Tree" (*fan-hun shu*). For further details, see the *Shiyi* (Supplementary Records).

The *Chuandu gu* (Poison-Coated Drum) in the *Guangzhi* states: "As for the *hen* bird, it is as large as a hawk; its neck is eight inches long, and its feathers are purple-green, covering its entire body."

This is poison. It takes snakes and vipers as its food; the male is named Huī and the female is named Yīn. If one drips wine onto their feathers and touches one's lips with it, death occurs instantly.
Rhinoceros horn is used to counteract it. This was the case when Wang Mang once administered poisoned wine to Emperor Ping. When it ascends into the air, the sun and moon lose their luster;
when it falls to the ground, all plants and trees wither. If people see it, their eyes go blind and sores break out; those who encounter its shadow lose consciousness.
When one dies, blood is used to smear upon a drum; whoever hears its sound will surely die. Only the "soul-returning incense" (*p'o-huan-hsiang*) can resolve this.
Thus, the Celestial Child said: "Having fully obtained the soul-returning incense, one nevertheless comes to strike the poison-smeared drum."
"Free from harm.
The *Zhan Guo Ce* records that the King of Qi sent an envoy to inquire after Zhao Wei Hou. Before the letter had even been opened, Wei Hou questioned the envoy, saying:
"Is the year free from harm? Are the people free from harm? Is Your Majesty also free from harm? The commentary states that "harm" (*yang*) refers to the venomous insect *yang*.
It is a worry. Furthermore, it is a parasitic insect capable of eating human hearts. In antiquity, when people lived in grass huts and slept in the open, many were afflicted by this poison;

thus, they inquired after one another’s welfare by asking, "Are you free from illness? Today, the common custom of asking about someone's ailment using the term "guì-yàng" (noble illness) is incorrect.

Regarding "lao-yan-long-chong" (the decrepit and frail), the *Zidian* states that "long-chong" is the name of a bamboo species produced on Mount Luofu. The *Danyanlu* states that long-chong resembles bamboo;
it sways and trembles, unable to support itself, much like an old person. Therefore, it is used as a metaphor. Master Shandao’s verse says: "Gradually..."

The skin becomes wrinkled like that of a hen and the hair turns white like a crane; look at how one’s gait grows faltering and decrepit. There is only the practice of the direct path: simply recite the name of Amitābha Buddha.
Having already attained [this state], one must guard against losing it.
The Master said, "Can a vulgar man be entrusted with serving his ruler? Before he has attained his position, he is anxious to obtain it; once he has obtained it, he is anxious to avoid losing it.
If he is truly anxious about losing it, there is nothing he will not do. The commentary states: "On a small scale, this means sucking at sores or licking hemorrhoids;
on a large scale, it means murdering one's father or one's ruler—all of which arise solely from the anxiety of losing what one has. (See *Analects*, Part II.)

"First the difficult, then the gain. Fan Chi asked about benevolence (*ren*). The Master said, "The benevolent person first undertakes what is difficult and only afterwards seeks gain; such a one may be called benevolent.

The commentary states that "gain" (*huo*) means acquisition. One prioritizes the tasks that are difficult and only afterwards considers the results obtained; this is the mind of the benevolent person.
This is seen in the *Analects*, Part One.

It is not necessary to be as inflexible as one who "glues the pegs" (to play the lute). Someone says: "To apply the laws of past sages to future times is like gluing the pegs of a lute while trying to tune it; does such a thing exist? He replies: "It exists."
It is said that sage-rulers are few while mediocre rulers are many; this is the case if one adheres solely to the Way of Zhongni (Confucius).
It is said that the laws of the sages have never failed to be connected with the rise and fall of dynasties. See the "Chapter on Prior Knowledge" in Yangzi’s *Fayen*.
"If you desire speed, you will not reach your destination.

When Zi Xia was serving as the magistrate of Ju Fu, he asked about government. The Master said: "Do not desire speed; do not look for small gains. If you desire speed, you will not reach your destination;
if you look for small gains, great matters will not be accomplished. (From the *Analects*, Part II)
Begging for leftovers when there was not enough, and looking elsewhere as well.
There was a man of Qi who lived with a wife and a concubine. Whenever his husband went out, he would invariably return only after having satiated himself with wine and meat.
His wife asked whom he had been eating and drinking with, and [the husband] replied that they were all people of wealth and status. His wife told her...
The concubine said, "I intended to observe where my husband was going. Rising early, I followed him from behind to see where he went.
Throughout the entire city, there was no one with whom he stood to converse. In the end, he was among those offering sacrifices at the mounds of the Eastern Enclosure.

He begged for the remains of the offerings; when there was not enough, he looked around and went elsewhere. When his wife returned, she joined her concubine in reviling her husband, and they wept together.
Regarding the phrase "in the middle courtyard," a direct explanation states: Mencius saw that those seeking wealth and honor at that time were acting with shame;
he therefore used a person from Qi as a pretext to illustrate this point. This is seen in detail in the *Li Lou* chapter of the *Mencius*.

"Acting with a view toward profit," the Master said. "Acting with a view toward profit leads to much resentment. The commentary states: "Fang (放) means 'to rely upon. 'Much resentment' refers to incurring much enmity.
This is found in the *Analects*, Part One.
"Human beings differ from birds and beasts by only a slight degree. Mencius said, "The reason why humans differ from birds and beasts is but a slight degree. The common people abandon it;
the noble person preserves it. The commentary states: "Slight degree" means few. "Common" means many. When human beings are born, they all equally receive from Heaven and Earth...
Principle constitutes one's nature; all alike receive the qi of heaven and earth to form their physical bodies. The common masses do not recognize this and depart from it;
thus, though they bear the name of "human," in reality they are no different from birds and beasts. The gentleman recognizes this and preserves it;
therefore, with constant wariness and self-motivation, he is ultimately able to fully realize the correctness of what he has received. Thus it is seen.
The Lower Part of Mencius. Chapter on Li Lou.
To distance oneself from Yang and Mo and to expel licentious discourse, Mencius said:
"Since the sage-kings no longer appeared, the feudal lords have become unrestrained and scholars-at-home have engaged in arbitrary debates. [Among them were] Yang Zhu and Mo Di."
"His words fill the world. Even until now, the doctrines of Yang Zhu and Mo Di have not ceased, while the Way of Confucius has not become manifest.

These are evil teachings that deceive the people and block the path of benevolence and righteousness. When benevolence and righteousness are blocked, then beasts will lead forth to devour men, and men will devour one another.
I fear this, and therefore I have guarded the Way of the former sages, resisted Yang and Mo, and expelled their licentious rhetoric, so that these evil speakers shall no longer [prevail]."

"It may be done. The commentary states: "Xián" (閑) means to guard; "fàng" (放) means to drive away to a distance; "zuò" (作) means to initiate. This is seen in the "Teng Wen Gong" chapter of the *Mencius*, Part One.

In the "Exhortation to the Crocodile" by Han Yu, it is said: "If a later king’s virtue is thin and he cannot exercise distant governance, then even the regions between the Yangtze and Han rivers are abandoned and left to the barbarians of Chu and Yue;
how much more so for the areas between Chao, Ling, and the sea, which are far removed from the capital?"
How vast it is! That the crocodiles have been submerged and incubating their eggs here is indeed their natural place. The commentary states:
"Submerged" means lying hidden; "incubating their eggs" means giving birth and breeding.

“Rectifying the Mind and Intent to Advance toward Bodhi.
The Preface to the *Complete Enlightenment Sūtra* by Prime Minister Pei Xiu states: "Alas! That by which sentient beings come and go are the six realms."
Furthermore, ghosts and spirits suffer the bitterness of profound obscurity; birds and beasts harbor the sorrow of frantic flight;
the asuras are in the midst of rage, while the devas are immersed in pleasure. Only through the human path can one rectify the mind and incline toward bodhi.
If a human being does not do so, there is truly nothing that can be done for them. Thus it is said.

The *Collection of Names and Meanings* regarding Xuanzang’s Westward Journey states: Xuanzang was a native of Luoyang in Henan. His secular surname was Chen; he was a descendant of Chen Zhonggong of Yingzhou.
He traveled throughout the Western Regions for seventeen autumns, visiting more than one hundred countries. This was in the nineteenth year of the Zhenguan era.
In the year he returned to the capital, an imperial decree was issued for him to translate over seven hundred sūtras and śāstras at Hongfu Monastery.
At that time, when Sudhana was traveling south in search of instruction, Mañjuśrī Bodhisattva addressed the youth Sudhana, saying: "O son of good family, if you wish to achieve..."
For the sake of the knowledge of all modes of omniscience (*sarvajñajñāna*), you should resolutely seek a true spiritual friend (*kalyāṇamitra*).

Noble son, in seeking a spiritual friend, do not give rise to weariness or indolence; upon seeing a spiritual friend, do not give rise to complacency; and regarding all the instructions of a spiritual friend, [do not disregard them].
You should all comply with this. Regarding the skillful means possessed by spiritual friends, do not look for their faults.
Son of good family, to the south of here there is a land called Sukhāvatī. In that land there is a mountain named Gṛdhrakūṭa (Vulture Peak).
There dwells a bhikṣu named Meghaśrī. You should go to him and ask: "How should a bodhisattva learn the bodhisattva conduct and cultivate it?"
"The conduct of a bodhisattva... even unto how one may swiftly bring the conduct of Samantabhadra to full perfection—Cloud of Virtue Bhikṣu shall explain this for you.
When the youth Sudhana heard these words, he was filled with joy and leaped for gladness.

He prostrated himself at his feet, circumambulated him countless times, gazed up at him with deep reverence, and wept with tears streaming down his face. Then, taking his leave, he traveled south toward Supratiṣṭhita.
In this manner, traveling successively through more than one hundred and ten cities, he paid homage to fifty-three true spiritual friends (*kalyāṇamitra*).
Finally, within the pore-porosity realm (*vairocana-keśa-raja-praveśa-kṣetra*) of Samantabhadra Bodhisattva, he sequentially attained the ocean of all practices and vows of Samantabhadra Bodhisattva.
He became equal to Samantabhadra and equal to all Buddhas, even unto inconceivable liberation.
Liberation and mastery are entirely equal. For a detailed account, see the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra*, fascicles 62 through 80.

The Great Master Huihan of the Wei dynasty, together with Kang Senghui, said: "When Senghui first arrived at Changgan, the Ruler of Wu, Sun Quan, commanded him to seek śarīra relics, setting a deadline."

He requested for seven days; [the Buddha] did not consent. He extended the request for twenty-one days; even at midnight, [the Buddha] still did not consent. Then he bowed his head and entreated him with grief, saying:
"The Buddha takes compassion as his heart. If you do not consent, you will cause the seeds of the Buddha to be severed and extinguished among the sentient beings of this region."

Thereupon, he fervently invoked the Buddha’s name three times. Blood and sweat gushed forth from every pore of his body, and immediately a resonant clanging sound was heard from within the bottle, its light illuminating heaven and earth. Upon opening it, the śarīra were found to be perfectly intact within the bottle.
(See *Jianmengyou ji*, scroll 25).
The Loss of the Sheep: A neighbor of Yangzi lost a sheep. He led his own followers and also requested Yangzi’s page-boy to pursue it.
Yangzi said, "Alas! You have lost but one sheep; why are there so many pursuers? The neighbor replied, "Because there were many diverging paths. When they returned...
He asked, "Did you find the sheep? He replied, "I lost it. He asked, "How did you lose it? He replied, "At the fork in the road, there was yet another fork;
I did not know which way to go, and so I returned. This is seen in the "Shuofu" chapter of the *Liezi*.
The *Qingnang* was seen by the simple woman named Hwa-t'o (Yuan-hua). She was a native of Chiao County in Pei State. Her skillful hands were rarely found in the world.
Once, while dreaming, Cao Cao was struck by the sword of a pear-tree deity; subsequently, his headache would not cease. He summoned Hwa-t'o to treat it. With...
Regarding the words of Ma Fei’s "Decapitating the Brain" (Pò nǎo), Cáo suspected him of treachery and had him seized and cast into prison.
The jailer treated Tuo very kindly, and Tuo, moved by his kindness, told him: "I am now to die an untimely death. I possess a book in a blue bag that has not yet been transmitted to the world.
I am deeply grateful for your kindness, but there is nothing with which I can repay it. I shall compose a letter; you must send someone to deliver it to me."
The man went home, retrieved the book, and handed it to him, saying, "This is a divine efficacy that shall continue my legacy.
The jailer said, "If I obtain this book, I shall abandon this service and treat the people of the world to fulfill the Master’s virtue.
Da then composed a letter and gave it to the jailer, saying, "When I was about to arrive, I entrusted this letter to my wife for her safekeeping. The jailer took his leave of Da.
He went to his home and asked Hwa-to’s wife for it. The jailer returned home and instructed his wife to hide it.
Ten days later, Cao’s illness grew even more severe, and Hwa-to died in prison. When the jailer was released from his duties and returned home, he asked his wife for the book.
The wife said, "I have already burned it. When her husband asked for the reason, the wife replied, "Even if one were to learn it, it would not be as good as Hwa-to's."
Duo Yiban met only with death in prison; therefore, I have condemned it. Consequently, the *Qingnang Shu* (The Green Bag Book) has not been transmitted to the world.
This is seen in the *Records of the Three Kingdoms*.
One rises when requesting instruction; one rises when a new topic is introduced.

When attending a teacher, if the teacher questions one, one answers only after the teacher has finished speaking. One rises when requesting a new subject of study; one rises when requesting further explanation.
The commentary states: "To 'request further instruction' means to rise again in order to inquire about matters not yet fully exhausted. One rises as a mark of respect.
When attending a gentleman while seated, if the gentleman changes the subject of conversation, one rises before responding. Lüshi (Lü Dajun) says:
"Rising to respond when the subject is changed is because there is a shift in the matter at hand, and thus one manifests reverence. These two points are found in the "Qu li" chapter of the *Li ji*.
The *Laṅkāvatāra-sūtra* states:

"Furthermore, Mahāmati, once a bodhisattva-mahāsattva has established himself in the characteristics of wisdom, he should diligently cultivate and study the three aspects of supreme noble gnosis (*āryajñāna*).
What are these three aspects of supreme noble gnosis that one should diligently cultivate and study?"

This refers to the mark of non-existence (*anupalabdhi-lakṣaṇa*), the mark of the sphere of the original vows of all Buddhas, and the ultimate mark of the noble wisdom of self-realization (*pratyātma-āryajñāna*).
Having attained this through practice, one is able to abandon the mental state and wisdom-marks of the "lame donkey" and attain the eighth stage of the Supreme Son (*jinaputra*).

The commentary states: "Having attained this through practice" refers to those of sharp faculties within the Shared Teaching (*sādhāraṇa-yāna*) who contemplate both emptiness and non-emptiness, and know the One.

Within the mind, these three characteristics are inherently present. "Being able to abandon the wisdom of the lame donkey" refers to transcending the wisdom of emptiness possessed by the two vehicles (śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas) of the Shared Teaching (sāmānyayāna).
The wisdom of the two vehicles that realizes the emptiness of essence merely functions within emptiness;
it cannot function simultaneously in both emptiness and existence, and is therefore called "lame. See *Lengqie yishu*, Scroll One, Middle Section.
When Vimalakīrti was thus rebuked,
Śāriputra saw that there were no seats within this room and thought to himself,
"Where shall these bodhisattvas and the great assembly of disciples sit? The elder Vimalakīrti, knowing his thoughts, spoke to Śāriputra.
He asked, "Venerable sir, have you come for the sake of the Dharma, or for the sake of a seat? Śāriputra replied, "I have come for the sake of the Dharma, not for the sake of a seat.
Vimalakīrti said, "Indeed, Śāriputra, one who seeks the Dharma does not cling even to body or life, let alone to things such as a seat.
Thus he rebuked him in various ways, as detailed in the second and third chapters of the *Vimalakīrtinirdeśa Sūtra*.
Scroll. The poem on the *mínglíng* from a different species says:
"The *mínglíng* has offspring; the *guǒluó* carries them away. The commentary states: "The *mínglíng* is a small green insect upon the mulberry tree."

The *bùqū* (mínglíng) is the *guǒluó*, a species of earth-bee. It resembles a bee but has a slender waist; it captures silkworm larvae and carries them into the hollows of trees, where they transform into its offspring after seven days.
Thus, when people today adopt children of a different surname as their own, they are said to be following the "mínglíng" method of raising an adopted son.
This is recorded in the "Xiǎowǎn" chapter of the *Xiǎoyǎ* section of the *Shījīng*.
In the sixteenth fascicle of the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra*, "The Ten Abodes," as taught by Dharmamati, the Bodhisattva Dharmamati arose from his meditative absorption and addressed the bodhisattvas, saying:
"O Sons of the Buddha, the dwelling places of bodhisattvas are vast, equal to the dharma-realm and space. Regarding those dwellings of the bodhisattvas, I shall now [explain]..."
I shall now speak. O Sons of the Buddha, there are ten stages in which Bodhisattvas abide.

These have been taught by the Buddhas of the past, will be taught by those of the future, and are being taught by those of the present. What are these ten? They are: the stage of the initial resolve, and so on, up to the tenth stage of consecration.
The *Vajragarbha-bodhisattva-daśabhūmi-sūtra*, the thirty-fourth fascicle of the *Avataṃsaka*. Bodhisattva Vajragarbha arose from samādhi and addressed the assembly of all bodhisattvas, saying:
"O Sons of the Buddha, the vows of the bodhisattvas are well-determined and unadulterated, for the sake of all..."
Protected by the Buddhas, one enters the ground of wisdom of all Buddhas of the past, future, and present.
Son of the Buddha, what is the ground of wisdom of the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattvas? Son of the Buddha, there are ten kinds of grounds of wisdom for Bodhisattva-Mahāsattvas.
Those of the past, future, and present Buddhas have spoken, will speak, and are now speaking them; I likewise speak them. What are they?
Ten [stages]: first, the Stage of Joy (*pramuditā-bhūmi*), up to the tenth, the Stage of the Dharma-Cloud (*dharmameghā-bhūmi*).

Regarding the "nine generations of kin," the *Yòuxué* (Youxue) says: "The nine generations of kin refer to the great-grandfather, grandfather, father, oneself, brothers, sons, grandsons, great-grandsons, and great-great-grandsons. The commentary states: "The father is called..."

*Kǎo*: The father of one’s father is called the *zǔ* (patriarch). The father of the *zǔ* is called the *zéngzǔ* (great-great-grandfather). The grandfather of the *zǔ* is called the *gāozǔ* (great-great-great-grandfather).

The son of a son is called a *sūn* (grandson). The son of a grandson is called a *zéngsūn* (great-grandson). The grandson of a grandson is called an *xuánsūn* (fourth-generation descendant). According to one interpretation, [the term] refers to the maternal grandfather.

One’s maternal grandmother, one’s wife’s father, one’s wife’s mother, one’s paternal aunt’s son, one’s paternal uncle’s daughter, one’s own daughter, as well as oneself and one’s kinsmen—these are practiced daily yet not examined.
As Mencius said: "To act without making it manifest, and to practice without examining it, one follows this throughout one's entire life."
"Those who do not know the Way are many. The commentary states: "The one who is attached knows it clearly; the one who observes recognizes it precisely.
Yet, while speaking of the practice, they cannot clarify what it is that ought to be so; having already become habituated to it, they still do not recognize why it is so.
This is why, throughout their lives, those who follow it without knowing the Way are numerous. See the "Jinxin" (Exhaustion of the Mind) chapter.

"Long-standing evils cannot be eliminated all at once. Huitang said: "That which has long been neglected cannot be perfected quickly; accumulated evils cannot be removed instantaneously. The commentary states:
"In all matters that have long been neglected, one must not pray for quick perfection; what is quickly perfected will surely be easily ruined. Accumulated maladies and defects..."
To abolish [customs] all at once leads to an increase in弊端 (corruptions). This is seen in the *Cānlín Bǎoxùn* (Precious Instructions from the Zen Forest).

Regarding the phrase "gradually and skillfully guiding," the *Lúnyǔ* (Analects) states: "The Master was gradual and skillful in guiding others; he broadened me with literature and constrained me with ritual. (Commentary follows.)
"Xunxun" describes an appearance of orderly progression; "inducing and advancing" means leading forward. "Extensive learning and concise ritual" represent the pinnacle of instruction.
This says that although the Master’s Way was lofty and subtle, his teaching of others followed a systematic order.

On Beating the Drum and Playing the Lute, National Teacher Zhong composed this verse: Beating the drum and playing the lute, He returns it to one who understands the family style. The wooden child is able to clap his hands.
A barren woman knows how to brew tea; clouds disperse and the moon appears at the edge of the sky. Spring comes and flowers bloom upon the trees;
Sudhana has visited every place, yet the black bean has not yet sprouted. Behold the thread that binds the Avataṃsaka.

When the autumn waters arrived, the River Lord [Hébó] was like a frog in a well. The hundred rivers poured into the river; the current of the Jing was so vast that between its two banks and its islands and shores, one could not distinguish an ox from a horse.
Thereupon, the River Lord was filled with joy and pride, believing that all the beauty in the world was entirely contained within himself.
Flowing eastward with the current, he traveled until he reached the Northern Sea. Facing east, he gazed, yet could not see the end of the waters.
Thereupon, the Lord of the River first turned his face around; looking out across the vast expanse toward Ruo, he sighed and said: "The common saying has it:
'To have heard but a hundred points of the Way, yet to think that none can equal oneself'—this describes me. Moreover, I have often heard that Zhongni was young."
...and thus you slighted the righteousness of Bo Yi. At first I did not believe this; now that I have seen how inexhaustible you are, had I not come to your gate, I would have been in peril.
I would have been constantly ridiculed by those of the Great Way. Bei Hai Ruo said:
"A frog in a well cannot be talked to about the sea, for it is confined to its pit. An insect of summer cannot..."
"To speak of ice is to be constrained by its season; a scholar of narrow views cannot be spoken to about the Dao because he is bound by his limited teachings.
Now you have emerged from the shore and observed the great ocean; thus you know your own insignificance. You may now be spoken to regarding the Great Principle.
This is seen in the "Autumn Floods" chapter of the *Zhuangzi*.

Mencius said: "Those who seek to subdue others by force do not win their hearts; it is because their strength is insufficient. Those who subdue others through virtue win them from the core of their hearts and achieve sincere submission.
The commentary states: *Zhan* means "sufficient. This speaks to the sincerity or falsehood of the hearts of the true king and the hegemon.

They are different. Therefore, the ways in which people respond to them are likewise different. Regarding the mother who gives birth and the foster mother, the teachings of the world recognize eight types of mothers:
first, the son born of a concubine refers to his father’s principal wife as his "legitimate mother" (*zhīmǔ*); second, the father’s concubine... [text continues].
1. One who has given birth to a son is called a *shùmǔ* (stepmother). 2. When three sons lose their mother, the father commissions another concubine who has no children of her own to care for them;

she is called a *címǔ* (foster mother). 3. One who suckles [the child] from infancy is called a *rǔmǔ* (nursing mother). 4. One who embraces and raises a child of the same clan, as well as a child abandoned at the age of three or younger, is called a *yǎngmǔ* (adoptive mother).
5. One whose father has died and whose mother has remarried to another family is called a *jiàmǔ* (remarried mother). 6. The seventh... [text fragment].

When one's mother dies and the father remarries, she is called a "stepmother" (jìmǔ). When one of the eight types of mothers has been defiled or estranged and is abandoned by the father, she is called an "expelled mother" (chūmǔ).
These details are found in the *Wénɡōn Jiālǐ* (Family Rites of Master Wén).
The father could not treat him as a son;
Xianqiu Meng asked, saying: "The ancient records state that for a man of such profound virtue, a ruler cannot treat him as a minister, nor can a father treat him as a son.
The commentary states: Xianqiu Meng was a disciple of Mencius; "the records" refers to ancient sayings. This is found in the section on Wan Zhang in the *Mencius*.
Chapter: The Buddha’s intention was not to accept his father’s prostration;
after the Buddha had first attained the Way, he converted the three brothers of the Kāśyapa clan. With a thousand bhikṣus, he traveled through the kingdom of Magadha and converted [others].
King Piṣā, about to return to his own kingdom, first dispatched Udāyin to inform King Śuddhodana: "In seven days from now, I shall come to convert you.
When the king heard this, he leaped for joy beyond measure and immediately ordered his carriage to be prepared and the roads to be leveled.
He swept and sprinkled the ground and burned incense, waiting for the Tathāgata. The Tathāgata thought to himself, "Now my father, the King, will surely come to welcome me.

I must not cause one so venerable to bend his body; I shall manifest my supernormal power (*ṛddhi*) and travel through the air at the height of a person's head, so that the King may receive me by taking hold of my feet.
The reason for this was that although the Buddha is honored in virtue, he did not wish to cause his parents...
This is because of the bending of the body. "One desires to stop but cannot" (*Lunyu*, Upper).
"The Master was methodical and excellent at guiding others: he broadened me with cultural learning and constrained me with ritual propriety. One desires—

"I am exhausted and can do no more. I have already exhausted my talents; yet it seems as though there stands something towering before me. Though I wish to follow it, I find no way to do so. The commentary states:
"Towering" describes the appearance of standing tall; "mo" means "none. This is Yanzi speaking of the extent of his own learning.
Indeed, because my joy is profound and my efforts are exhausted, that which I perceive becomes ever more intimate, yet there is no further application of effort required.

I prostrate myself and take refuge in the *Zhou Li* (Rites of Zhou), specifically the Great Invoker (*Da Zhu*) of the Ministry of Spring, who distinguishes the protocols of the nine types of salutation. The first is the *jiexiu* (prostration with the head to the ground); the second is the *dun*... [text truncated]

1. *Shǒu* (Prostration): Bending the head to touch the ground. 2. *Sānkōngshǒu* (Triple Prostration): Bending the head down until it reaches the hands; this is what is called *bài shǒu* (bowing with the hands). 3. *Zhèndòng* (Vibrating Prostration):
A prostration performed with trembling and physical agitation. 4. *Jíbài* (Auspicious Prostration): Performing the bow first, followed by the touching of the forehead to the ground (*jīmiǎng*).

5. *Xiōngbài* (Inauspicious Prostration): Touching the forehead to the ground first, followed by the bow. 6. *Qíbài* (Odd Prostration): This refers to a single prostration. 7. *Báobài* (Reciprocal Prostration): This refers to performing two prostrations.
The ninth is the *sùbài* (prostration with a bow). This involves merely lowering the hands; in modern times, it has been raised [to a full prostration]. The *Anleji Shuchao* states:

"Taking refuge (*guīmìng*) follows the pattern of the *pāramitās*; it is a form of inverted speech. There are two meanings of 'taking refuge' (*guī*): first, the meaning of surrendering and entrusting oneself. It is said that for worldly people, nothing is more precious than body and life.
To offer up one's body and life in taking refuge represents the height of sincerity and reverence, being free from any dualistic mind. Second,"
The meaning of "returning to the source" is to take refuge with one's entire body and life, comprehensively gathering the six sense faculties and returning them to the single mind.

The *Shi Jing* (Book of Poetry), in the poem "Bi-fei Gan-tang," states: "Lush and verdant is the sweet pear tree; do not prune it, do not cut it down; it was where the Earl of Shao took shelter. The commentary notes: "Bi-fei" describes the appearance of flourishing abundance.

The *gāntáng* is the *dùlí* (pear-tree). Those that are white are called *táng*; those that are red are called *dù*. "To prune" means to trim its twigs and leaves; "to cut down" means to fell its branches and trunk.
"The Duke" refers to the Regional Duke (*fāngbó*). "At the grass-hut" (*bài*) refers to a shelter made of grass.

When the Duke of Shao traveled through the southern states to disseminate the governance of King Wen, he sometimes stayed beneath the *gāntáng* trees. Later generations, remembering his virtue, came to cherish these trees.
Yet one cannot bear to harm it. This is seen in the "Sweet Pear Tree" (*Gāntáng*) chapter of the *Gāngfēng* (National Airs) in the *Zhāonán* (Southern Marches).
Regarding the Way of Ultimate Sincerity, the *Zhōngyōng* (Doctrine of the Mean) states:
"The Way of ultimate sincerity can allow for foreknowledge. The commentary explains: "Sincerity (*chéng*) refers to being truly real and without falsehood; 'ultimate' (*zhì*)..."

This is truly what is meant by the substance of the Sage’s virtue. However, it is only when sincerity reaches its ultimate perfection—such that not even a trace of private artifice remains within the mind or eyes—that one is able to perceive the subtle movements of things (*ji*).

Regarding the saying, "The words are near, but the meaning points far," Mencius said: "Words that are near yet point to what is far are excellent words; principles that are concise yet yield broad application are excellent paths.
The speech of the gentleman does not descend below the belt, yet the Way is contained therein. The commentary states: "The ancients did not look downward."
Regarding the "girdle": it refers to that which is upon the girdle, the place most immediately before one's eyes.
By taking up this immediate matter before us, the ultimate principle is found therein; thus, the words point to what is near in order to indicate what is far. See the "Exhausting the Mind" chapter.
The Tathāgata, by means of his supernormal power, merged them into a single bowl.
As the Sūtra says: "At that time, when the Tathāgata was about to accept the food of those merchants, he reflected:
'All past Buddhas have held bowls; with what vessel should I now receive this food? Having had this thought,"
At that time, the Four Heavenly Kings brought forth bowls made of the seven precious substances and offered them to the Tathāgata; however, the Tathāgata did not accept them.
Then, King Vaiśravaṇa addressed the other heavenly kings, saying: "In the past, there was a Heavenly King with a blue body who brought four stone bowls and gave them to us.
Furthermore, another deity came and said to me: 'Be careful not to use these bowls; they should be used for making offerings.'"
The perception of a stūpa. Why is this? In the future there will be a Buddha named Śākyamuni; one should offer this bowl to that Buddha.

Desiring to bestow the stone bowl, now is precisely the right time. At that time, the Four Heavenly Kings, holding that stone bowl filled with celestial flowers, came to where the Buddha was and said:
"World-Honored One, we pray only that the Tathāgata will accept this bowl from us. [He] accepted it.
[This was] human food. At that time, the World-Honored One thought to himself: "The Four Great Heavenly Kings have offered me these almsbowls with pure faith.
However, it is not fitting for me to possess four bowls. If I were to accept only one, the others would surely feel resentment. I shall now accept all four bowls;
having accepted them, I will stack them one upon another and press them down with my hand so that they merge into a single vessel, with its four rims [remaining distinct]."
It is clear. At that time, the Tathāgata recollected the past and spoke this verse:
"In the past, I filled a bowl to the brim with flowers and offered it to immeasurable Tathāgatas; therefore, the Four Heavenly Kings now bestow upon me this firm and pure bowl.
This is found in detail in the tenth fascicle of the *Mahāvyūha-sūtra*.

The lively verse says: "The kite flies up to heaven; the fish leap in the deep pool. This speaks of its being observed from above and below. The commentary states: This is from the "Hanzu" chapter of the *Dà yǎ* section of the *Shī jīng*.
The "kite" (*yuán*) belongs to the class of hawks and owls. "Lì" means to arrive at. "Chá" means to be manifest. Master Cheng said: "This one section [is the teaching of] the Master..."
Reflect deeply on the point of acting for others with urgency; it is vital and lively. May the reader apply their thoughts to this. See the *Zhongyong*:
"Words have a source, and affairs have a master.
Master Hanshan’s commentary on the "Free and Easy Wandering" chapter of the *Zhuangzi* states: "Zhuangzi himself said that words have a source and affairs have a master."
"O Lord, this is precisely the fundamental principle of establishing one's doctrine. However, these words do not appear in the Inner Chapters; perhaps they originate from the Outer Chapters.
It is a pity that I have not yet seen them; let us await further investigation."
Master Quan cited the twentieth fascicle of the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra*, which says: "When that infant cries, his parents immediately take yellow leaves from a willow tree and say to him:
'Do not cry, do not cry; I shall give you gold. Upon seeing this, the infant—"
Conceiving the thought that it was genuine gold, he immediately ceased crying.
Good son, just as that infant conceived the thought of genuine gold regarding what was not gold, so too does the Tathāgata speak of purity within impurity.
Because the Tathāgata has attained the ultimate truth (*paramārtha*), he is without falsehood.

Regarding his teaching others without weariness, the Master said, "As for being a sage or a man of perfect virtue, how could I dare claim such? However, that I never tire of practicing them and never weary of teaching others—this is all I can say.
Gongxi Hua said, "This is precisely what I, your disciple, am unable to learn. The commentary states:

This, too, is a humble expression of the Master. A Sage is one who has attained greatness through transformation; "benevolence" (*ren*) is the perfection of the heart’s virtue and the completeness of the human way.
To "practice it" means to act according to the Way of benevolence and sagehood; to "instruct others" likewise means to teach people by means of this.
Yet, to be neither weary nor indolent in doing so is impossible unless one has already internalized it oneself. This is why the disciples—[could not... (the text here is fragmentary).
"One is able to learn. Seen in the *Lunyu* (Analects), Volume One. △ Volume Four:
Bodhisattva Dharaṇīdhara Waits for the Buddha on Level Ground.
The *Śūraṅgama Sūtra*, fascicle five, states: Bodhisattva Dharaṇīdhara prostrated at the Buddha’s feet and addressed the Buddha, saying:
"I recall that in the past, when the Tathāgata Samantaprabhā appeared in the world, I was a bhikṣu.
I constantly repaired all major roads, ferry crossings, fields, and narrow passes where they were improper or uneven, causing damage to carts and horses; I leveled and filled them all. Or..."
I constructed bridges or carried sand and earth. During the time when Vipaśyin Buddha was in the world, the great king of that country invited the Buddha to a vegetarian feast.
At that time, I leveled the ground to await the Buddha. Vipaśyin Tathāgata rubbed the crown of my head and said to me:
"You should level the mind-ground; then the ground of the world will all become level."

The *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra*, in its nineteenth fascicle, states: "Udraka Rāmaputra attained the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception and possessed the five supernormal powers (*pañcābhijñā*).
Day after day, he would fly into the royal palace to eat. According to the laws of that kingdom, the king’s consort would receive him by touching his feet in prostration."

When his feet touched the ground, his desire arose and he lost his supernormal powers (*abhijñā*). Seeking a carriage, he returned to the mountain and practiced the five supernormal powers once more. With single-minded devotion, he later attained meditative concentration (*samādhi*) as before and was reborn in the Heaven of Neither Perception nor Non-Perception (*naivasaṃjñānāsaṃjñāyatana*).

Regarding the phrase "without front or rear" (*wúzú xiānzhì*) in the *Xiǎoyǎ*, the sixth month chapter of the *Shī* states: "My chariot is secure; it is as if tilted forward, as if tilted backward. The commentary notes: "Tilted forward" (*zhì*) refers to the chariot overturning toward the front;

"tilted backward" (*xiān*) refers to the chariot leaning toward the rear. Generally, when viewing a chariot from behind, it appears as if tilted forward... [From here, the text continues with the description of the chariot's appearance from various perspectives.]
Viewed from the front, it appears as if tilted forward; only then is it properly balanced. The *Biography of Ma Yuan* in the *Book of the Later Han* states:

"When in front, he could not cause others to lean backward; when behind, he could not cause others to lean forward. "Leaning forward" (*xuan*) means lightness; "leaning backward" (*zhi*) means heaviness. This says that in his conduct as a person, he did not cause others to be perceived as either light or heavy.

The transformation of conduct and the refinement of customs are described in a poem: "Solemn is the rabbit snare; It is set with a rhythmic thud-ding-ding. Stout and brave are these warriors; They are the bulwark and wall of the dukes and marquises. The commentary states: "Snare" refers to a net.

When the transformation of conduct spreads and customs are refined, the multitude of worthy talents is such that even the commoners who set rabbit snares in the wilds [possess such virtue]. Even their...

The utility of talent is thus. Therefore, the poets used the subjects at hand to evoke imagery and praise them, whereby the flourishing of King Wen’s virtuous transformation can be perceived. This is seen in the *Guofeng*, "Zhounan."
"To do well by a task, one must first sharpen its tools.
Zeng Gong asked about the practice of benevolence (*ren*). The Master said, "A craftsman who wishes to do well by his work must first sharpen his tools.

When living in a state, serve those among the high officials who are worthy and befriend those among the scholars who are benevolent. The commentary states: "Worthy (*xian*) refers to their conduct in service."
"Ren" is spoken of in terms of virtue. The Master once remarked that Zigong delighted in those who were not his equal;
therefore, he informed him of this, wishing for him to have someone to revere and fear, and through mutual refinement, to perfect his virtue. This is seen in the *Analects*, Part One.
The Quail Mocks the Great Peng:
The "Free and Easy Wandering" chapter of the *Zhuangzi* says: "There is a bird whose name is Peng. Its back is like Mount Tai; its wings are like clouds hanging from the heavens.
It strikes up upon the whirlwind (the *fúyáo* and *yángjiǎo*) and ascends ninety thousand *lǐ*, passing beyond the vapors of the clouds and bearing the azure sky."
"O Heaven! Only then shall you plan to go south—to the Southern Ocean. The quail (a small bird of the marshes) laughed at him, saying:
'And where does he intend to go? I leap up and fly no more than a few *ren* before descending again, soaring among the *peng* and *hao* weeds;
this too is the height of flight. So, where does he intend to go?'"
The Verse on the Vows and Practices of Samantabhadra from the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra*, the eldest son of all Tathāgatas, is named the Honored One Samantabhadra.
I now dedicate all my roots of goodness, wishing that all my wise practices may become identical to his.

"Even in moments of haste or distress," the Master said, "the gentleman does not for even the duration of a single meal depart from benevolence (*ren*). In moments of haste he must remain therein; in moments of distress he must remain therein. The commentary states:

"A single meal" refers to the brief interval of one sitting at a meal. "Moments of haste" refers to times of urgency and improvisation. "Moments of distress" [refers to times of being overturned or thrown into turmoil].
In moments of collapse and exile, one speaks of the junzi practicing benevolence;

from the choices between wealth and honor or poverty and meanness, down to the intervals of a single meal or the briefest moments of haste and distress—there is no time or place where his effort is not applied.
In the *Analects*, Volume One, it says:
"The transformation by timely rain.
Mencius said: "There are five ways in which a gentleman instructs others; one is like being transformed by a timely rain. The commentary states: [as above].

"Timely rain" refers to rain that falls at the proper season. When grasses and trees grow, and when seeds are sown and cultivated, human effort has already been exerted, yet they cannot transform themselves on their own;
what they lack is merely the nourishment of rain and dew. If it rains at such a time, their transformation occurs swiftly.
The subtle art of instructing people is also like this. See the "Jinxin" (Exhaustion of Mind) chapter in the *Mencius*.

"Minutely cautious and composed": The *Analects*, in the "Xiangdang" chapter, states: "When the ruler was present, he was minutely cautious and composed. The commentary notes: "When the ruler was present" refers to the time of the morning audience.
"Minutely cautious" (*zuzi*) describes an appearance of reverent unease; "composed" (*yuyu*) describes an appearance where one's dignified demeanor is perfectly appropriate.

Regarding the statement in Zhang Shangying’s *Fahulun* (Treatise on Protecting the Dharma), "The dog of Shun barks at Yao": Confucians know only the Way of Confucius and Mencius, yet those who exclude Buddhism are what is meant by the term "the dog of Shun.
Shun had a dog that barked when Yao passed by his gate; this was simply a dog—it was not intended as a metaphor.
That Shun was good while Yao was not so is because one has commonly seen Shun, whereas one has not commonly seen Yao;
this is seen in the *Dharmapāla-śāstra*.
On hearing on the road and repeating on the road, the Master said: "To hear something on the road and repeat it on the road is to cast away one's virtue. The commentary states:
"Though one hears virtuous words, if one does not make them one's own, this is to cast away one's virtue oneself. See *Analects*, Part II.
All are but the trap and the snare.
As the "External Objects" chapter of the *Zhuangzi* says: "The trap exists for the sake of the fish; once the fish is caught, one forgets the trap.
The snare exists for the sake of the rabbit; once the rabbit is caught, one forgets the snare. Words exist for the sake of the meaning; once the meaning is grasped, one forgets the words. I—
How could one find a person who has forgotten words with whom to speak?
