Upon reaching Penglai, the waters were again clear and shallow. Ping remarked, "The Eastern Sea has once more become as dry as dust. I have seen this in the *Leishu Chuanyao* (Essential Excerpts from Categorized Books).

Regarding the supreme dignity of the "Ninth Yang" (Jiuyou), the *Yi Jing* says: "The Ninth Yang: A flying dragon is in the heavens; it is advantageous to see the great man. The commentary states: "The strong line is established in the center and the correct position, thereby occupying [the throne]."
Regarding the honorable position: it is like one who, by virtue of the sage’s moral excellence, occupies the sage’s station; thus its image is as described.
See the Qian hexagram in the *Zhouyi*:
"A common man becomes a teacher for a hundred generations."

The Epigraph for the Temple of Han Mungong in Chaozhou states: "That an ordinary man may become a teacher for a hundred generations, and a single word may become a law for all under heaven—this is because he has participated in the transformations of Heaven and Earth and governed the cycles of prosperity and decline."

"Be kind to the people and love all things. Mencius said: "The gentleman’s attitude toward things is one of love, yet not of benevolence; his attitude toward the people is one of benevolence, yet not of intimacy.
He practices intimacy toward his kin, benevolence toward the people, and love toward all things. The commentary states: "Things refers to birds, beasts, plants, and trees."
"Affection" (愛) means taking [one's parents] at the proper time and using them with moderation; this is seen in Mencius, Volume 1, Part 2, "The Chapter on the Exhaustion of Mind.
Furthermore, all who possess vital breath know how to honor and love [their parents], as cited in the first volume, Part 2. Their fame and reputation overflowed, as quoted therein.
Zu Gong said, "Clever words and a pleasing countenance constitute excessive courtesy. Zu Qiu Ming felt ashamed of this; I, too, feel ashamed. The commentary states:
"Zu" means "excessive. Zu Qiu Ming was a man of renown in antiquity. Xie Shi remarked: "This which is shameful is even worse than [the aforementioned]."
This refers to those who break through walls or climb over fences. Zu Qiu Ming felt shame for such acts; thus, one can discern the character of his upbringing.

The Master himself said, "I, Qiu, also feel shame for this," likely intending to compare himself to Lao Peng by way of humility, while also providing a profound warning to students to examine this matter and establish their hearts with integrity.
This is recorded in the *Analects*, Part One.

Regarding "using loyalty to extend [the principle] to oneself," the *Zhongyong* says: "Loyalty and extension are not far from the Way. It continues: "What you do not wish done to yourself, do not do to others.
The commentary states: "To exhaust one's own heart is loyalty; to extend oneself to others is extension. 'Vi' (違) means to depart. This means that if one is already able..."
To exhaust one's own heart and further extend oneself to others, one will not be far from the Way.

The two lines beginning with "What you do not wish for yourself" concern the practice of loyalty and reciprocity (*zhong-shu*). Since the heart of oneself and the heart of others have never been different, that which one does not desire for oneself should not be extended to others.
If one acts thus in all matters, after a long time, will one not advance toward [the Way]?
Is this the Way?

My heart rushes toward the towers of Wei, where the Zhou rites are preserved. The *Tianguan Dazai* (Great Minister of the Ministry of Personnel) states: "Then hang the laws of administrative governance upon the *xiangwei*. The commentary says: "The *xiangwei*..."
This is missing from the text. The *Yùnhuì* states: "Two towers are erected outside the gate, with multi-storied pavilions atop them;

the upper part is circular and the lower part is square, and because the laws are suspended there, they are called *xiàngwěi*. 'Xiàng' refers to the 'images of governance' (the penal codes). 'Wěi' describes their appearance as being lofty and imposing."
It is tall and large. It was made for the people to gaze upon; thus it became known as a "gaze-point" (guàn). Two towers are planted side by side, with no gate between them.
Furthermore, palace gates, bedroom gates, and tomb gates may all be called *què* (gate-towers).

The weeds *láng* and *yǒu* bring harm to the fine grain; as the *Shijing* says: "Neither *láng* (pronounced láng) nor *yǒu* (pronounced yǒu); remove the *míng* and *tè* (pronounced tè), and also the *móu* (pronounced móu) and *zé*.

Let them not harm the young seedlings in my fields. The commentary states: "*Láng* refers to *tóngliáng*; *yǒu* resembles the sprout. Both are weeds that damage the sprouts. That which eats the heart [of the grain] is called..."

The *míng* (locust) eats the leaves; the *téng* (grasshopper) eats the roots; the *móu* (cricket) eats the joints; and the *zé* (insect) [eats the stalks]. These are all insects that harm the seedlings.
"Zhì" refers to young rice plants. This means that once the seedlings have flourished, one must further eliminate these four types of insects before the rice in the fields can be free from harm.
This is seen in the "Dàtián" chapter of the *Xiǎoyǎ*.
△ Scroll Five. Carrying bribes in bundles, filthy and impure, wagging their tails to beg for pity.
Ying of Shaowu said to Huìtáng: "In the Dharma-ending age, bhikṣus do not cultivate morality or virtue; those with even a modicum of integrity and righteousness are few. He went on...

"In the past, they wrapped themselves in bribes and filth, wagging their tails to beg for pity. The commentary states: "Bao-ji" (苞苴) means "wrapped packages"; "ang-zang" (骯髒) refers to the appearance of the body as it coils and turns.
This speaks of monks of the Final Dharma (mofa) who do not cultivate the Way nor nourish virtue, and furthermore cannot maintain integrity or uphold righteousness;
they frequently wrap up rare items to present to those in power, seeking to solicit favors, just like a dog that wags its tail upon seeing a person.
To flatter them with one's tail is merely to seek their pity. Having read the *Baoxun* (Precious Instructions) and its commentary, I recall the passage from the *Analects*:
"Only women and petty men are difficult to sustain; draw near to them and they become insolent; keep them at a distance and..."

"Enmity. The commentary states: "When a gentleman presides over his ministers and concubines with dignity and nurtures them with compassion, he will be free from the troubles caused by these two groups. See the *Analects*, Part II.

Regarding the phrase "picking out flaws like blowing on fur" (*chuīmáo qiúzhī*) from the *Yòuxué*: "One must examine even minor transgressions, as if blowing on fur to seek out flaws. The commentary states:
During the reign of Emperor Wu of the Han, there was a proposal to suppress the feudal princes by reporting their faults and evils; this was described as "blowing on fur to seek out flaws."

Regarding the lines from the *Qi'ao* chapter of the *Wei Feng* (Wind of Wei) in the *Shi Jing* (Book of Poetry): "As if cutting, as if sawing; as if carving, as if polishing. The commentary states: This refers to the *Qi'ao* chapter of the *Wei Feng*.

"Cutting" is done with knives and saws; "carving" is done with chisels and drills; both involve shaping materials to form their substance and appearance. "Sawing" is done with burnishers and files; "polishing" is done with whetstones.
"Sand and stone are used to treat materials so that they become smooth and lustrous. As for what is said regarding the treatment of bone and horn:

"having cut them, one further planes them"; regarding the treatment of jade and stone: "having carved them, one further polishes them. All these express that once the treatment has already reached a high degree of refinement, one seeks even greater refinement. This is seen in the *Daxue*.

When Zixia asked, "The skillful smile is radiant; the beautiful eyes are dark and bright; with plainness as the ground, the colors are displayed—what does this mean? the Master said, "In painting, the white ground comes last.
Zixia said, "Does this not mean that ritual (*li*) comes last? The Master said, "You have stimulated my thoughts, Shang! Only now can you truly participate in my discussions."
The discussion of poetry has concluded. The commentary states: "It inspires me," meaning it is able to arouse and develop my own aspirations and intentions;

this is seen in the *Analects*, Part One. When Mencius instructed King Xuan of Qi, he said: "Now, if Your Majesty issues policies and practices benevolence, you will cause all those in office throughout the world to desire to stand in Your Majesty’s court;
all those who farm to desire to till the fields of Your Majesty; and all merchants and traders to desire to store their goods therein."
The king’s marketplace and his travelers all wish to exit by the king’s road; those throughout the world who are dissatisfied with their ruler all wish to come to him for redress.
When it is thus, who can resist him? The King said: "I am muddled and cannot advance in this regard.
I pray that you, Master, assist my will and instruct me with clarity. [Commentary: "Muddled" (*hūn*) is the same as "dull" (*hūn*). "Assist my will" means to aid my resolve.
This refers to guiding one's aspirations. See Mencius, "The Chapter on King Hui of Liang.

Regarding the phrase "recognizing the bubble while discarding the ocean," the second fascicle of the *Śūraṅgama Sūtra* says: "It is like [discarding] hundreds of thousands of vast, clear oceans and recognizing only a single floating [bubble]."

The substance of the bubble is designated as the entire tide, exhausting the vastness of the ocean. The commentary states: "That sutra uses this as a metaphor for abandoning the true and recognizing the false, while further taking the false to be the true.

Now, I have briefly borrowed its phrasing in this sub-commentary to illustrate how clinging to the provisional (the skillful means) violates the ultimate reality; it is not that I am adopting its specific meaning."

Regarding the taking of hailstones for pearls, a verse from the *Aṅgulimālīya Sūtra* says: "Suppose there is a foolish person who, seeing hailstones, gives rise to a false imagination, thinking they are lapis lazuli beads.
Having taken them, he carries them home and places them inside a jar or vessel, guarding them as if they were genuine jewels. Before long, they all completely melt away."
One forms the conceptualization of emptiness while remaining in silence. One likewise forms the conceptualization of emptiness regarding other true lapis lazuli. The commentary states:

the first six lines of that sutra metaphorically represent ordinary beings who cling to the conditioned as real; the subsequent two lines metaphorically represent the followers of the Two Vehicles who perceive the conditioned as empty.
The latter two lines serve as a metaphor for the Two Vehicles not seeking the fruit of Buddhahood. Now, we do not adopt that interpretation;
rather, taking hailstones for pearls serves merely as a metaphor for the Two Vehicles clinging to provisional means as if they were the ultimate reality.

A poem from the *Gāndhārī* (or *Kangxi*) states: "The stalwart warrior is the bulwark of the dukes and marquises. The commentary notes: "Stalwart" (*jiǎojiǎo*) describes a martial appearance; "bulwark" (*gān*) refers to a shield.

Both the bulwark and the city wall serve to ward off external threats and protect what is within. This is seen in the *Zhōu Nán* chapter of the *Guófēng* (Odes of the States). Furthermore, the *Zuǒzhuan* says:
When the Way prevails in the world, princes and dukes can serve as shields and bulwarks for the people.
According to the "Lü Wēng’s Dream of the Yellow Millet" (Lǚwēng Jīng): On the road to Hándān, within an inn, there was a young man named Lú Shēng who lamented his own poverty and distress.

The youth rested his head on it and dreamed that he arrived in a kingdom where he achieved fame and office to his heart's content;

he experienced wealth and nobility for over fifty years before growing old and sick, passing away. As he yawned and stretched, he awoke to find the old man standing by his side, while his host was still boiling the yellow millet.

[The Master] replied, "It is still not yet ripe. Shēng thanked him, saying, "Master, you have used this to block my desires. [This is recorded in] the *Yìwén jí*. When Zhòngní saw Wēnbó Xuězǐ, he did not speak. Zǐlù said, "The Master wished to see Wēnbó Xuězǐ but remained silent. Zǐlù asked, "Why was that? in terms of spiritual capacity (*indriya*), the lesser sage falls short of the ordinary person. This concludes the section on Resolving Doubts, titled "The Arising of the Sage."
To avoid being eaten by ants:
When Zhuangzi was about to die, his disciples wished to give him a lavish burial. Zhuangzi said, "I shall take heaven and earth as my inner and outer coffins;
the sun and moon as my paired jade discs; the stars and constellations as my pearls and gems; and the myriad things as my funeral offerings. Are these funeral requisites not sufficient?"
"Is this sufficient? Why add more to this? The disciple said, "I fear that crows and ravens will devour the Master.
Zhuangzi said, "Above, it becomes food for crows and ravens; below, it becomes food for ants. To take from those and give to these—how partial you are!
(See the *Lie Yukou* chapter of the *Zhuangzi*).

They vow to be born in that land, yet they do not understand the Buddha’s wisdom; their minds remain hesitant and wavering. Only when their lives are ending do they repent for their own faults, and by virtue of this, they are born there.
As soon as they enter the peripheral lands, they see a city of the seven treasures and immediately settle there, being born from within a lotus flower.
There is also natural happiness, such as that of the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven; yet, even while dwelling within that city for five hundred years, one cannot see the Buddha nor hear the Dharma.

This clarifies the meaning of the superior grades of excellence. Regarding the two lines concerning the gradual late blooming of the lotus:

those born in the middle grade of the superior level have their lotuses bloom after one night has passed, and they immediately behold the Buddha. Those born in the lower grade of the superior level have their lotuses bloom after one full day and night;

Zhuangzi was escorting a funeral procession.

Passing by the tomb of Huizi, he looked back at his attendants and said, "When a man of Ying had plaster smeared upon the tip of his nose like the wing of a fly, he asked me, Master Shi, to chisel it away.
Master Shi brandished his adze with such force that it created a whirlwind; listening for the slightest sound, he struck, and the plaster was completely removed."
The plaster was applied and his nose was not injured; the man of Ying stood there without losing his composure.
When Lord Yuan of Song heard of this, he summoned the artisan Shi and said, "Try, for my sake, to chip away at it. The artisan Shi replied, "I was indeed once able to do so.
However, the 'raw material' for my work has been dead for a long time. Since the death of that Master, I have had no material to work upon, and I have no one with whom to converse."
This is recorded in the "Miscellaneous Chapters" of the *Zhuangzi*.
When Cook Ding was disassembling an ox for Lord Wenhui, his eyes saw no whole ox;
he allowed his blade to roam freely. Wherever his hands touched, wherever his shoulders leaned, and wherever his feet trod—
The parts where his knees were tucked in all moved in perfect harmony with the musical rhythm. Lord Wenhui said, "Aha! How wonderful! Can skill truly reach such a state?
Cook Ding set down his knife and replied, "What I cherish is the Way; it goes beyond mere skill.
When I first began to dismember oxen, there was nothing before my eyes but oxen. Three years later, I no longer saw the ox as a whole."
It is further said: "Those joints have spaces between them, while the edge of the blade has no thickness. To enter those spaces with what has no thickness—how vast it is!
There will surely be ample room for the blade to move. This is seen in the "Care for the Lord of Nourishing Life" chapter of the *Zhuangzi*.

Regarding the fact that the various devas eat from the same vessel yet differ in the coarseness or excellence of their food, the seventh fascicle of the *Qishi yinben jing* (*Sūtra on the Causes and Origins of the World*) states:

"When a celestial son or celestial daughter is first born, due to the habitual conditioning of their own karma, three thoughts arise: first, they know for themselves from which place they died; second, they know for themselves..."

They know that they have been born in this place. Thirdly, they know by what karma and what meritorious retribution they were born here—namely, because they cultivated wholesome conduct through body, speech, and mind, they obtained rebirth in this place. Having formed this thought, they then contemplate food.
When they think of eating, there appear before them various jeweled vessels, naturally filled with divine *sudarśana* food of various different colors.
Among the sons of the gods, those who possess superior karma have *sudarśana* food that is the most pure white in color.
Regarding those with middling karmic retribution, their color is somewhat reddish. Those with inferior merit have a somewhat blackish complexion.
Once it enters the mouth, it dissolves of its own accord, like butter cast into fire, leaving no further form or shadow. When they are thirsty, [the water] appears right before them.

There are divine jeweled vessels filled to the brim with celestial wine; according to whether one's merit is superior, middling, or inferior, it appears white, red, or black, and upon entering the mouth, it dissolves away, no different from before.

According to the *Juntian Shi*, Duke Mu of Qin dreamed that he went to the abode of the Emperor and beheld the grand music of Juntian. The Emperor bestowed upon him a decree, and consequently, the state of Qin flourished greatly.

This is so. The commentary states: "A single body" is like a single limb. "Possessing the whole body but in miniature" means that while the entire body is present, it has simply not yet expanded.
See the Gongsun Chou chapter of the Mencius, Part One.

he instructed them to drive it while looking toward the south, so that they might know the path back home. The compass used today is a remnant of this device.
This is a compilation. It appears in the *Lieguo zhuan* (Biographies of the Warring States).

The *Rākṣasa-darśana-aviparyaya-parīkṣā* states:
There was a man who, upon seeing anything extraordinary, would invariably question it. Later, while traveling through a vast wilderness, he encountered a rākṣasa.
He seized him. When the man saw himself being seized, he was certain to die. However, seeing that the rākṣasa’s chest was white and its back was black, he asked in wonder about the reason for this.
The rākṣasa replied, "Since my birth, I have had no liking for seeing the sun; therefore, I always walk with my back to the sun, which is why the front is white and the back is black.
The man understood his meaning and quickly pulled back the rākṣasa's hand, then ran toward the sun. The rākṣasa, however, could not face the sun.
Seeing that the man had escaped, he spoke this verse: "Diligent study is the foremost path; diligent inquiry is the foremost method.
When encountering the peril of a rākṣasa on the road, turn your back on the shade and face the bright sun."

In the twenty-second year of Duke Zhuang of Lu, in the spring, the first month of the year, there was a general amnesty for major offenses (*si da sheng*). The commentary states: *si* means to release; *sheng* means offense.
To release and pardon major offenses is like the modern-day imperial pardon (*she-shu*), wherein all great crimes are entirely granted clemency. The *Chunqiu* specifically [records this].

The *Shu* (Book of Documents) records that a general amnesty was granted for major offenses during the interval between the death and burial of Wen Jiang. This is seen as praise for Duke Zhuang’s ability to remedy his transgressions;
see the *Pingce Yiyi*, Volume Six, on the *Zhuang Gong* commentary of the *Chunqiu Zuozhuan*.
The Tang Dynasty prohibited flogging on the back; the "Junzi" (gentleman) praised Emperor Taizong for his preservation of benevolence.

When Emperor Taizong of the Tang read the *Mingtang Zhiyan Shu* (Book of Acupuncture and Moxibustion of the Hall of Brightness), he noted: "The connections of the five viscera are entirely attached to the back.

He subsequently issued an edict stating that from now on, no prisoner shall be flogged on the back. The commentary states: "The 'Junzi' refers to the historian who records these words. It means the historian chronicled this.
The prohibition against flogging on the back during the Tang dynasty was likely intended by the gentlemen of the historical records to praise Emperor Taizong’s compassionate intent;
it followed as swiftly as a shadow follows a form or an echo follows a sound.

What is called "bringing peace to all under heaven" lies in governing one's own state. When the superior honors the elderly, the people are inspired to practice filial piety; when the superior honors the elders, the people are inspired to practice fraternal respect;
when the superior shows compassion for the orphaned, the people do not turn their backs on them. Therefore, the gentleman possesses the way of the "measuring square. The commentary states:

these three matters show that when the superior acts above, the subordinates follow below, as swiftly as a shadow follows a form or an echo follows a sound. This is what is meant by "the family being brought to order," and...

Regarding unfiliality, there are three things that are greater than having no descendants;

Regarding these matters: first, to flatter and pander to others' whims, thereby leading one's parents into unrighteousness; second, to refuse to serve for a salary when the family is poor and the parents are elderly;
third, to remain unmarried and childless, thereby severing the ancestral sacrifices. Among these three, the failure to provide descendants is the greatest offense.
See the "Li Lou" chapter of the Mencius.

Discussing the Way was sufficient for his own delight. He wished that the Honorable and Just One would govern the world with impartiality, so that the seasons might be harmonious and the years bountiful;
thus, Tong would receive much grace. He died, and his posthumous title was Wénzhōngzǐ (Master of Literary Virtue). Sháo Yōng was a native of Hénán during the Sòng dynasty.

Regarding the Three Dukes (*sān tái*), Zhu Xi’s *Collected Annotations on the Elementary Learning* (*Xiǎoxué jízhù*) states: "In the Zhou dynasty, the Grand Preceptor (*tàishī*), the Grand Tutor (*tàifù*), and the Grand Guardian (*tàibǎo*) were the Three Ducal Ministers (*sāngōng*).

In the Eastern Han, the Commander-in-Chief (*tàiwēi*), the Minister of Education (*sītú*), and the Minister of Works (*sīkōng*) were the Three Ducal Ministers. The *Treatise on Astronomy* (*Tiānwén zhì*) states: "The Three Terraces (*sāntái*) consist of six stars, arranged in two pairs."

Turning westward, the two stars near *Wenchang* are called the Upper Terrace (*shàngtái*); the next two stars are the Middle Terrace (*zhōngtái*); and the two stars to the east are the Lower Terrace (*xiàtái*).
In human society, they correspond to the positions of the Three Dukes (*sāngōng*). The *Zhèngzìtōng* states: "The name 'Three Terraces' (*sāntái*) refers to the stars;

furthermore, 'Terrace' (*tái*) and 'Tripod' (*dǐng*) are titles for the Three Dukes. This is like the stars having three terraces and a tripod having three legs. Furthermore, [there was] King Wu of Qin.

In the first year of his reign, he first established the position of Chancellor (Xiang-heng). Furthermore, there were the Counselors (Fu), the Assistants (Bi), and the Vice-Counselors (Yi-Cheng), collectively known as the Four Auxiliaries (Si-fu).

Those who assisted me by complementing my actions were called Fu; those who corrected me by brushing away my errors were called Bi; those who deliberated before me were called Yi; and those who supported me from behind were called Cheng.
Moreover, there are celestial bodies named the Four Auxiliaries; these four stars assist the North Pole Star.

The *Yijing* commentary *Yi jiao bu zhu* states: "Calculating and measuring" (*tui bu*) refers to observing the geography of the earth from below; "fullness and emptiness" (*ying xu*) refers to observing the celestial phenomena of the heavens from above.
Furthermore, "calculating and measuring fullness and emptiness" means calculating and measuring the fullness and deficiencies of Heaven and Earth.

Regarding the wife of a feudal lord, the *Analects* states: "The wife of a feudal lord is called 'the Lady' (*furen*) when the lord refers to her; she refers to herself as 'the Little Child' (*xiaotong*)."
The people of his own state address her as "Lady" (jun-furen). When addressing her to other states, they call her "Our Small Lady" (gua-xiaojun).
People from other states also address her as "Lady."

The *Zuǎnlíngjì* states: Wang Minggān of Jīngzhào was originally devoid of virtuous conduct and had never cultivated goodness.
When he died of illness, he was led by two men to the gate of hell. There he saw a monk, who said he was Kṣitigarbha Bodhisattva. Thereupon—
The instructional verse says: "If a person wishes to fully understand all Buddhas of the three periods of time, they should contemplate in this way: the mind creates all Tathāgatas.
After the Bodhisattva had bestowed the sutra upon him, he said, "By being able to recite this verse, you shall be able to cast off the sufferings of hell.
Once the man had finished reciting it, he entered the king's presence. The king asked the man, "What merit do you possess? He replied, "I have merely upheld one..."
Having recited the four-line verse as above, the king then released him. At the moment he was reciting the verse, all those suffering in the places reached by the sound attained liberation.
Only after three days did he regain consciousness; remembering and upholding this verse, he spoke it to both monastics and laypeople.
Upon examining the verses, one comes to know that these were spoken by an immeasurable assembly of bodhisattvas gathered in the Yāma Heaven Palace within the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra*;
they are the verses of Bodhisattva Ghoṣadatta. The final two lines of the current text state: "One should contemplate the nature of the dharma-realm."

A single bowl of fragrant food can satisfy an ocean-like assembly.
The Vimalakīrti Sūtra states: At that time, the transformed bodhisattva offered a bowl filled with fragrant food to Vimalakīrti.
The fragrance of this food pervaded the city of Vaiśālī as well as the trichiliocosm. Then Vimalakīrti addressed Śāriputra and the other great śrāvakas, saying:
"Venerable ones, you may eat. This is the ambrosial meal of the Tathāgata, permeated by great compassion. It is inexhaustible.
He ate it with a restricted mind so that it would not be digested. There was another śrāvaka who thought, "This food is meager.
The manifested bodhisattva said, "Do not, by means of the small virtue and small wisdom of a śrāvaka, attempt to measure the immeasurable merit and wisdom of the Tathāgata.
The four oceans may run dry, but this food is inexhaustible. Even if all people were to eat it, taking mouthfuls as large as Mount Sumeru, for as long as an eon, it would still not be exhausted."

It was able to be exhausted. Why was this? For those who are fully endowed with the inexhaustible virtues of precept, concentration, and so forth, that which remains after they have eaten can never truly be exhausted.
Thus, the rice in the bowl satisfied the entire assembly, yet it was still not depleted.
Those bodhisattvas and śrāvakas who ate this food felt their bodies become peaceful and joyful.

"When you see the worthy, think of emulating them. The Master said: "When you see the worthy, think of emulating them; when you see those who are not worthy, examine yourself within. The commentary states:

"The various officials shall consolidate their duties and listen to the *Zhongzhai*. The commentary states: "*Zhong*" means "head" or "eldest. In ritual, there are such designations as the "eldest son" (*zhòngzǐ*) and the "eldest wife" (*zhòngfù*);

the people of the Zhou dynasty also referred to the chief minister as the *Zhongzhai*. In ancient times, when the King was in mourning for his parents, the *Zhongzhai* presided over the ancestral sacrifices.

He presides over the ancestral temple and the various officials each attend to their own duties while awaiting the instructions of the Grand Chancellor; thus he presides over the assembly of ministers.
This is recorded in the "I Xun" chapter of the Shang Shu.
The *Pusa bai ze mituo shu chao* states: There is a divine beast named Baise (White Deer) that can speak human language and discerns the true nature of all things;
all malevolent spirits flee upon seeing its shadow. Therefore it is said: "If a household possesses a chart of the Baise, such demonic apparitions will certainly not exist."
Regarding "Going to Another Country Without Relatives," the *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya* states: The Buddha addressed the bhikṣus: "In a past age, there was a kingdom named Vārāṇasī.
At that time, there was a great and filial Brahmin named Bhāradvāja who served as the royal preceptor. He was constantly instructing five hundred disciples. At that time...
A certain Brahmin had a slave named Kāla. Having heard the sound of the Dharma being preached, he was able to memorize it all.
Once, while with some young boys, he felt a slight resentment and departed for another country, falsely claiming, "I am the son of the Brahmin Puluhe.
The National Preceptor was greatly pleased and said to him, "I have a daughter; I shall now give her as a wife to you. He replied, "I accept."

[He was] a teacher. That man was constantly angry regarding food and drink. His wife thought to herself, "If someone should happen to come from the kingdom of Vārāṇasī, I shall receive instruction from him.
When the Great Brāhmaṇa heard this matter, he immediately departed for another country.

When that man learned of it, he went at once to pay his respects, saying, "I have come to this country and claim to be the son of the Great Master. I hope you, my lord, will not reveal this matter. My Lord—
He said, "You are truly my son. Immediately, he returned home with his master and announced, "My kinsman has arrived; let us prepare food and drink for him.
His wife asked the Brahmin in secret, "My husband’s meals are always to his displeasure; I pray that you, Venerable Sir, will instruct me.
He replied, "When I was about to depart, I taught you a verse. That man is seeking a companion as his host; at that time, my lady, please request the verse from him. And so it was.
He instructed her, saying: "Do not go to another country and deceive the people of the world. Coarse food is our constant sustenance; why then be angry over fine food?
His wife reflected on these verses, and because that man always spoke with gentle words, she never again gave rise to anger.
